AFTER: Did you know that 1 in 3 of those visiting food banks are children? Food Banks Canada's After The Bell program provides nutritious, child-friendly food packs throughout the summer when school-centered supports are not available so kids can soar on the swings and splash in the community pool with their friends. Participating food banks receive packs that contain shelf-stable items such as milk, hummus, crackers, cereal, oatmeal and sunflower seeds and they also receive grant money to supplement the food packs. The goal in 2024 is for the program to deliver 200,000 packs in 215 communities across Canada.
AGAIN: "On the Road Again" was a beloved Canadian television show that aired from 1987 to 2007 on CBC! Hosted by the iconic Wayne Rostad, the show traveled across Canada, showcasing the unique stories and traditions of everyday Canadians in towns big and small. Each episode celebrated the diverse cultures, landscapes, and people that make Canada so special.
ALGAE: Algae thrive in Canada’s waters, from the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes and all the way to the Pacific. Green Cladophora in the Great Lakes supports fish and helps monitor water quality, while coastal seaweeds like rockweed shelter marine life along British Columbia’s shores. These simple organisms are unsung heroes, keeping Canada’s freshwater and marine ecosystems healthy.
ALTAR: Canada has several famous altars, mostly found in its historic churches and cathedrals. These altars are known not just for their religious significance but also for their architectural and artistic beauty. A few notable examples include the altars at Notre-Dame Basilica and Basilica of Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, and the St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica altar in Toronto. These altars not only serve as the focal points for worship but also stand as significant artistic and architectural landmarks in Canada's religious and cultural landscape.
ANTHEM: Canada’s national anthem, O Canada, was first performed in 1880 in Québec City and has since become a defining part of our shared identity. Originally written in French, an English version followed in 1906, with its lyrics continuing to evolve for more than a century. In 1980, Canada’s National Anthem Act received royal assent and officially took effect on July 1, becoming a centerpiece of that year’s Dominion Day celebrations. Whether sung in schools, at hockey games, or during national ceremonies, O Canada remains a moment that unites Canadians from coast to coast to coast.
ANVIL: Anvil is a Canadian heavy metal band formed in Toronto in 1978. The band currently consists of founding members guitarist/vocalist Steve "Lips" Kudlow and drummer Robb Reiner, along with bassist Chris Robertson who joined in 2014. As of 2022, the band has released nineteen studio albums; they have been cited as having influenced many notable heavy metal groups including Megadeth, Slayer, Anthrax, and Metallica.
APRON: Wok with Yan was a Chinese cuisine cooking show starring Stephen Yan that was first produced in Vancouver, British Columbia in the late 1970s. It ran until 1995 with over 500 episodes, and each show featured Yan wearing of an apron with a different pun on the word "wok." The humorous aprons complemented his humour that consisted of spontaneous one-liners and playing with the food & cookware. "Wokkey Night in Canada" is our absolute favourite apron!
ARMED: Canadian Armed Forces Day takes place on the first Sunday in June each year and is a celebration of the members of the Canadian Armed Forces, both those who are currently serving and those who have served in the past. To all current and past members of the Canadian Armed Forces, and to the loved ones who stand with you, we appreciate and recognize your bravery, dedication and sacrifice. Thank you for answering the call to serve, and for making Canada and the world a better place to live.
ARRAY: The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) is the world's next-generation radio-astronomy observatory. Currently under construction, the SKAO will operate the 2 largest radio-telescope arrays in the world. The observatory is a global collaboration with partners on 5 continents and in both hemispheres, and Canada has been a key partner since the 1990s, contributing to its design, construction, and scientific use. Canada will be home to one of the SKA's regional centres, which will be part of the SKA Regional Centre Network.
ARROW: Canada's response to the threat of Soviet nuclear bombers was the Avro Arrow. A marvel of engineering, it was a twin-engine, all-weather supersonic interceptor. Only five Avro Arrow planes were ever built, yet this innovative jet fighter put Canada on top of the aviation world in the 1950s.
ASTER: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! The aster is a vibrant, star-shaped wildflower that brightens Canadian meadows and gardens from late summer into fall. With over 20 native species in Canada, asters provide an important source of nectar for bees and butterflies, supporting pollinators across the country. Traditionally linked with love, patience, and elegance, it’s a fitting bloom to celebrate and honour mothers everywhere on Mother's Day.
ATLAS: The Armstrong Whitworth Atlas was a British single-engine two-seat biplane. It served as an army co-operation aircraft for the Royal Canadian Air Force in the 1920s and 1930s. April 1, 2024 marked 100 years of service for the Royal Canadian Air Force as a distinct military element. The RCAF Centennial is an opportunity to showcase Air Force personnel and their accomplishments, demonstrate air and space power, enhance the reputation of the RCAF, and proudly honour its distinguished history and heritage.
ATTIC: Attic Records was a Canadian independent record label, founded in 1974 by Alexander Mair and Tom Williams. The label was known for developing Canadian talent, including Anvil, Lee Aaron, Maestro Fresh Wes, The Nylons, Teenage Head, and Triumph. The company was also active in distributing international acts not affiliated with a major label, most successfully with Jennifer Warnes, "Weird Al" Yankovic, Katrina and the Waves, and Creed.
AXLES: Canada’s early auto industry relied on strong, durable axles to keep vehicles rolling across rugged roads. In the 1920s and 1930s, factories in Ontario and Quebec built cars and trucks with heavy-duty axles that could handle both city streets and rural trails. These simple yet vital components were essential to the growth of Canada’s automotive industry and its expanding national transportation network.
BACON: Canadian bacon comes from the loin of the pig instead of the side or belly.
BALLS: Canada's athletes have excelled in a variety of ball sports, making their mark on the Olympic stage! From softball to baseball, racquetball to handball, basketball to volleyball, soccer to beach volleyball, and goalball, sitting volleyball and wheelchair basketball in the Paralympics, Canadian teams and individuals have showcased their talent and determination. A few notable performances include the Canadian women's softball team winning bronze at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, and John Child and Mark Heese winning bronze in beach vollyeball at the Atlanta 1996 Olympics. With successes across these ball sports, Canadians have truly shown their skill and versatility in the Olympic arena!
BANJO: The Banjo Bowl is the annual rematch game between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders of the Canadian Football League after the Labour Day Classic. The game has been sold out every year since 2005. As of the 2023 season, Winnipeg leads the series 12–7. The Blue Bombers will host the CFL's Western Final this Saturday, after the team secured the top spot in the division for the third season in a row.
BARNS: Canada is home to countless barns scattered across its vast agricultural landscape, serving as iconic symbols of rural life and farming heritage. Barns have played a crucial role in Canada's agricultural history, providing shelter for livestock, storage for crops, and a place for farmers to work and gather. From the iconic red barns of the Canadian prairies to the picturesque white barns of rural Quebec, each barn tells a story of hard work, resilience, and connection to the land. When you're driving through the countryside, keep an eye out for these charming structures that stand as enduring symbols of Canada's agricultural heritage.
BATON: Canada has a strong tradition of excellence in relay races, with its teams achieving notable success on the world stage. The Canadian men's 4x100m relay team famously won gold at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, a triumph that echoed the country's prowess in track and field. More recently, the men's 4x100m team clinched silver at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, further solidifying Canada's status as a powerhouse in relay events. These achievements highlight the strength and teamwork that define Canadian athletics.
BEANS: Baked beans are one of Canada’s truly national dishes – beginning with Indigenous iterations all the way up to its place on pulse trends of today’s Canada’s food guide. And while many ingredients are incredibly regional, the versatility and history of the humble bean spans from coast to coast. Our favourite style is fèves au lard, a traditional Québécois dish of beans mixed with pieces of bacon and either molasses or maple syrup that is then slow cooked in the oven. Delish!
BEAVER: The beaver is one of Canada's most iconic animals! Once vital to the fur trade that shaped the country's early history, it became a national symbol of industry and perseverance. In 1975, the beaver was officially recognized as Canada's national animal. You can even spot this hardworking rodent on the Canadian nickel!
BEERS: Canadians spent $9.2 billion on beer in 2020 ($325 per adult), which equates to 2.3 billion litres of beer.
BENCH: In the House of Commons, MPs with leadership roles sit on the front bench, while everyone else sits on the back bench. Backbenchers may not wear the cabinet title, but they’re far from idle, reviewing legislation in committees, introducing private members’ bills, and taking part in Question Period. In the 45th Canadian Parliament, all 343 MPs, including the backbench, keep the work of democracy moving every day.
BERRY: It's berry season in Canada! The start of summer means an abundance of fresh strawberries, raspberries, blueberries, blackberries and Saskatoon berries. The Saskatoon berry shrub is native to western Canada and has been an important food source for those inhabiting this landscape for thousands of years. In fact, the name Saskatoon is derived from the Cree word ‘Mis-sask-quah-too-mina’ for the berry producing plant.
BINGO: The game of Bingo has been a beloved pastime in Canada for decades! In fact, the first official Canadian Bingo hall opened in the 1940s in British Columbia, and the game quickly became a popular way to raise money for charities, schools, and local communities. Whether played at a community centre or as a family game night favourite, Bingo remains a fun way to bring Canadians together! From coast to coast, Canadians have enjoyed shouting "Bingo!" as a way to win big and support their communities at the same time.
BLESS: Canada is home to a unique maritime tradition known as the 'Blessing of the Fleet'! Each year in Digby, Nova Scotia, locals gather to participate in this special ceremony, which dates back over a century. The blessing of the scallop and deep sea fishing fleet is a time-honored tradition where fishermen and their vessels are blessed by clergy for a safe and bountiful fishing season. This event not only celebrates the rich maritime heritage of Nova Scotia but also serves as a symbol of community unity and support for those who make their living from the sea. It is a cherished tradition that brings together residents and visitors alike to offer prayers and well-wishes for the fishermen and their families.
BLITZ: Today is the 110th CFL Grey Cup! When you hear the term blitz you probably think of football, but The Canadian Wildlife Federation and the Nature Conservancy of Canada use Bioblitzes to help determine the health of an ecosystem. A Bioblitz is a participatory search for species within a limited area and a limited timeframe that takes a "snapshot" of as many living things as possible. Biodiversity - literally the variety of life - is an indicator that an area is ecologically stable and healthy. Through use of the iNaturalist Canada app, the species records are compiled into a single data set to help researchers, scientists and policy-makers to help them make informed decisions about wildlife management.
BONES: Known as the "Dinosaur Capital of the World", the town of Drumheller, Ablerta has some of the richest deposits of fossils and dinosaur bones in the world! In Alberta's Red Deer River valley, home to Dinosaur Provincial Park, more than 1,000 complete skeletons of extinct dinosaurs have been found since the late 1800s.
BOWER: The word bower comes from the classic card game Euchre, a longtime favourite in Canada! In Euchre, the "right bower" (jack of the trump suit) and "left bower" (jack of the same colour) are the top two cards. With its simple rules, quick rounds, and team play, Euchre has become a go-to game in homes, cottages, and legion halls across the country. It's a true staple of Canadian card culture!
BOXES: Boxing Day in Canada has a unique blend of traditions! While it originally involved giving “Christmas boxes” to workers and those in need, today, Canadians also embrace it as a day for major shopping sales and hockey. From filling donation boxes for local charities to watching Team Canada in the World Juniors, Boxing Day is all about generosity and community spirit - true Canadian values!
BRAID: Although the cultures and traditions of Indigenous Peoples are diverse, the importance of long hair is the same for all Nations. It is a long-standing practice within many First Nations for both women and men to wear their hair in braids. It is seen as a symbol of their connection to culture and Indigenous roots. For some, braids are a symbol of strength and wisdom, and it represents a connection to their ancestors, the Earth and the Creator.
BRAVE: On November 11th, we remember and honour all the individuals who have and continue to serve in Canada's military services. Attending Remembrance Day ceremonies on November 11th is a well known way to honour the brave men and women who served Canada in times of war, military conflict and peace. For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those brave soldiers who fought for our country and made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
BRAVO: In the Canadian military, "Bravo" is more than just an exclamation of praise; it's the code word for the letter "B" in the NATO phonetic alphabet, which ensures clear communication across the Canadian Armed Forces and beyond. The phonetic alphabet - from "Alpha" to "Zulu" - is used worldwide, helping Canadian military personnel coordinate and reduce misunderstandings during missions. Bravo is also commonly used to name companies within various units like the Bravo Company, 1st Battalion, The Royal Canadian Regiment (1 RCR) Battle Group. Additionally, the term Bravo Zulu (BZ) is also a naval signal meaning "well done", and is commonly used across all branches to commend service members for a job well executed.
BREED: Canada is home to several unique dog breeds that reflect its history and climate. The Canadian Inuit Dog, also known as qimmiq, is the official animal of Nunavut and has long been used for sledding across Arctic terrain. The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a clever and energetic hunter, was developed in the Maritimes to lure and retrieve waterfowl. The Newfoundland, strong and skilled in swimming, helped fishermen in coastal waters, while the Labrador Retriever, originally from Newfoundland, was bred to assist fishermen by retrieving nets and fish. These Canadian breeds showcase skill, resilience, and a special bond with people across the country.
BRINE: Brine isn’t just salty water – it’s the starting point for one of Canada’s biggest salt success stories. At its Goderich operation on Lake Huron, Sifto Canada operates the world’s largest rock salt mine, producing millions of tonnes of bulk salt each year. A separate nearby facility pumps up underground brine, then evaporates and refines it into around 95,000 tonnes high-purity, food-grade salt each year. From seasoning kitchens to preserving food across the country, Canadian brine plays a quietly essential role at the table.
BRUIN: The bruin, or bear, is a creature deeply connected to Canada’s wilderness. Black bears roam across most of the country – with more than 380,000 estimated in Canada – while brown bears, including grizzlies, wander the west. From the dense forests to the rugged mountains, the bruin remains a powerful symbol of Canada’s vast and untamed landscapes.
BULBS: Today marks the start of the 2024 Canadian Tulip Festival in Ottawa, with over 100 tulip varieties and more than one million blooms over 14,000 m². The Festival preserves the memorable role of the Canadian troops in the liberation of the Netherlands and Europe, as well as commemorates the birth of Dutch Princess Margriet in Ottawa during World War II - the only royal personage ever born in Canada. Each year, the Netherlands continue to give 20,000 bulbs to Canada as a gesture of gratitude. In 2001, the tulip became Ottawa’s official flower.
BULLS: Bull riding is a popular and exhilarating event at the Calgary Stampede, one of Canada's largest and most famous annual rodeos! Every year, rodeo enthusiasts and thrill-seekers from around the world flock to Calgary, Alberta, to witness the heart-pounding action of bull riding, where riders attempt to stay on a bucking bull for an eight-second ride. Canada is also home to the Professional Bull Riders (PBR) Canada circuit, where some of the toughest and most talented bull riders compete for glory. With events held in cities and towns across the country, PBR Canada brings the excitement of bull riding to fans from coast to coast.
BURNT: Dr. Wilder Graves Penfield was one of Canada's foremost neurosurgeons. He had a desire to understand the cause of brain illnesses, and made groundbreaking advances in the treatment of seizure disorders. Penfield established the Montreal Neurological institute (the Neuro) in 1934, and along with his colleagues, developed the Montreal procedure for patients with severe epilepsy. The first patient to undergo the Montreal procedure reported smelling burnt toast, and this helped doctors to identify and destroy the nerve cells causing the seizures. Penfield’s experiments with stimulating different parts of the brain helped us learn to map its different sensory areas. Check out this Heritage Minutes video about Dr. Wilder Penfield to learn more!
BURST: The countdown is on to 2024! In skies across Canada and around the world at midnight tonight, there will be fireworks bursting and producing beautiful displays of light and colour to ring in the new year. Cheers to the New Year!
BUSBY: A busby is a tall fur hat traditionally worn by cavalry and hussar regiments, as well as certain artillery and rifle units in the Canadian Armed Forces. Designed originally for mounted soldiers, the busby is a distinctive symbol of cavalry heritage. The Royal Canadian Dragoons, Canada’s senior cavalry regiment, historically wore the busby in the late 19th century but now wear a brass dragoon helmet with a black plume for full dress. Today, the busby remains an important part of full dress uniform for many Canadian military regiments, honouring their rich traditions and mounted roots.
BUTTE: Situated in the Big Muddy Badlands in Saskatchewan, Castle Butte is a grand, reddish free-standing structure with a circumference of 0.5 km and an elevation of 60 metres. A relic from the Ice Age, it is a striking formation that served as a landmark for Indigenous people, the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) and early prairie settlers. Other notable Canadian buttes include Pilot Butte (Saskatchewan), Lone Butte (British Columbia), Nebogwawin Butte (Manitoba), Nahanni Butte (Northwest Territories), and Mud Buttes (Alberta). It goes without saying that these buttes are some of our country's finest assets! Read more about Canada's Nicest Buttes.
CACHE: Geocaching is the real-world treasure hunt where participants use GPS satellites and coordinates to hide and retrieve containers or caches hidden in outdoor locations. There are millions of caches all around Canada! In Ontario, deep in the Haliburton Highlands in the Municipality of Highlands East and at the South Gate of Algonquin Park a string of seven hamlets make up the Geocaching Capital of Canada: Irondale, Gooderham, Tory Hill, Wilberforce, Harcourt, Highland Grove and Cardiff. Get out there and explore!
CACTI: Four species of cacti are native to Canada: pincushion cactus, little prickly pear cactus, common plains prickly pear cactus, and eastern prickly pear cactus. All of these species are at the northern limits of their distribution. In 1985, the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada officially designated the cactus as an endangered plant.
CAJUN: Happy National Acadian Day! On August 15, we celebrate the culture, history, and resilience of Acadian communities across Canada. After the Deportation of the Acadians in the 1700s, many were exiled from their Maritime homeland. Some eventually settled in Louisiana, where the word “Acadian” evolved into “Cajun.” While Cajun and Acadian cultures have distinct histories, Cajun traditions remain a vibrant reminder of Canada’s Acadian roots – rich in music, food, language, and pride that still echoes from the Maritimes to the bayou.
CANDY: Did you know that Ganong candy company in St. Stephen, New Brunswick is Canada's oldest chocolate and candy company? Canada is also home to some unique sweet candy treats, like Smarties, Coffee Crisp, Caramilk, Aero, Crunchie, and Mackintosh's Toffee to name a few!
CAPES: Canada is home to some stunning coastal landscapes adorned with picturesque capes! Along its vast coastline, Canada boasts numerous capes that offer breathtaking views of the surrounding seas and landscapes. One iconic example is Cape Breton Island's Cabot Trail in Nova Scotia, where rugged cliffs meet the Atlantic Ocean, creating a dramatic and awe-inspiring vista. Cape Scott Provincial Park on Vancouver Island is renowned for its remote wilderness and rugged coastline, while Cape Columbia located on Ellesmere Island in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut is the northernmost point of land of Canada and offers incredible views of the Canadian Arctic. Cape Spear in Newfoundland and Labrador holds the distinction of being the easternmost point in North America. Canada's capes provide endless opportunities for adventure and discovery!
CEDAR: Canada has the world’s largest stock of standing western redcedar trees. The western redcedar is the arboreal emblem of the province of British Columbia.
CELLS: Stem cells were first discovered by Canadians Dr. James Till and Dr. Ernest McCulloch who were both pioneers in biomedical research. Stem cells can self-renew and can be artificially grown, leading to all kinds of possibilities for the cure of disease and the rebuilding of tissue. Till and McCulloch were jointly nominated and inducted into the Canadian Medical Hall of Fame.
CHAIN: Did you know that a group of lynx is called a "chain"? The Canada lynx, a native species to Canada, is known for its distinctive tufted ears and large, padded paws that act like snowshoes in the winter. These elusive cats are most commonly found in the boreal forests of Canada, where they primarily hunt snowshoe hares. While lynx are typically solitary animals, the term "chain" is used to describe a group of them when they do come together. Seeing a chain of lynx in the wild is a rare and remarkable sight, reflecting the rich biodiversity of Canada's wilderness.
CHALK: Chalk River Laboratories is a Canadian nuclear research facility in Deep River, about 180 km north-west of Ottawa. It is a site of major research and development to support and advance nuclear technology, particularly CANDU reactor technology. Until the shutdown of its nuclear reactor in 2018, CRL produced a large share of the world's supply of medical radioisotopes.
CHEST: Our chest rises and falls with every breath - something we often take for granted. Respiratory therapists across Canada are the experts who help keep those breaths strong and steady. Represented by the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists (CSRT), they care for people with conditions affecting the lungs and chest in hospitals, communities, and beyond. This week from October 19-25, the CSRT celebrates Respiratory Therapy Week, honouring the dedication and vital work of Canada’s respiratory therapists!
CHICK: Happy Easter from Canuckle! From chocolate treats to springtime farm visits, the chick is a beloved Easter symbol across Canada. These fluffy little birds represent new life and fresh beginnings - perfect for a holiday that celebrates renewal, hope, and the arrival of spring. They're a cute reminder of the season's fresh start!
CHIME: The Peace Tower’s 53 bells chime high above Parliament Hill, ringing out everything from O Canada to classic folk tunes. Played like a giant piano, this grand carillon is one of the largest in the world! Since 2008, Canada’s official Dominion Carillonneur, Dr. Andrea McCrady, has performed thousands of live recitals from the tower, keeping this uniquely Canadian tradition ringing loud and proud in the heart of Ottawa with every chime.
CHIPS: Canadians love their potato chips! In 2020, the Canadian potato chips market had total revenues of almost $2 billion. Canada is also home to some truly Canadian original flavours - both Ketchup and All Dressed chips are almost exclusively available in Canada!
CHOCK: A chock is a wedge used to keep wheels or sleds from rolling, and in Canada’s snowy north, chocks are essential for sleds and dog teams. Chocks can be made of wood, rubber, metal, plastic, or even ice, helping adventurers and mushers stay safe on slippery trails. This simple tool proves that even the smallest pieces can have a big impact in the great outdoors!
CHORD: Canada has a long tradition of bringing musicians together, and Four Chords & The Truth is one of the country’s most beloved showcases for songwriters. Launched in Toronto in 2015, this unique event invites artists to share their music “in the semi-round,” taking turns performing songs and telling the stories behind them. The result is an intimate night where every chord struck carries a bit of truth – a perfect harmony of Canadian creativity and storytelling.
CHUTE: The Canadian Forces Parachute Team, the SkyHawks, is Canada’s only military parachute demonstration team. It has been representing Canada and the Canadian Forces for more than 50 years, providing parachute demonstration jumps to over 75 million spectators worldwide under the team’s signature Canadian flag parachutes.
CIVIC: Canadian citizens have the civic duty to serve on a jury if called to do so and the civic responsibility to vote in Canadian elections. Federal election voter turnout in Canada rose sharply in the 2015 federal election to 68.3% of eligible voters, the highest turnout since 1993. Voter turnout decreased to 67% in 2019 and to 62.2% in 2021.
CIVIL: Canada History Week 2023 takes place from November 20 to 26. This year’s theme is the History of Black Achievement in Canada. The week encourages Canadians to reflect upon and engage with Canada’s past. Viola Desmond was a Canadian civil and women's rights activist and businesswoman of Black Nova Scotian descent. In 1946, she challenged racial segregation at a cinema in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, by refusing to leave a whites-only area of the Roseland Theatre. Viola was forcibly removed and jailed, sparking the civil rights movement in Canada. #HistoryWeek2023
CLAIM: Today is National Indigenous Peoples Day! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Gertrude Guerin was a fierce protector of Indigenous people and culture. Living near Vancouver, Guerin spent her adult life helping the Indigenous Peoples of the city. From founding Indigenous organizations, to serving as chief of her First Nation, to helping launch a landmark land claims case, Gertrude had a huge impact on the Lower Mainland area and Canada. The Supreme Court decision in the Guerin case is one of the most important legal judgments in the history of Indigenous law in Canada.
CLERK: The Clerk of the Privy Council is the professional head of the Public Service of Canada. As the deputy minister for the Privy Council Office (the Prime Minister's department), the clerk is the senior civil servant in the Government of Canada and serves as the secretary to the Cabinet.
CLIFF: Baffin Island, Canada is home to Mount Thor, the world's tallest vertical cliff. In fact, it's steeper than vertical, with a 105-degree overhang. Check out this article by Jeopardy champ Ken Jennings all about Mount Thor!
CLOWN: Richard Pochinko (1946–1989) was a notable Canadian clown trainer who developed a new style of mask/clown performance training, known as the "Pochinko Method" or the Canadian Clowning technique. Originally from Selkirk, Manitoba, he was based primarily in Toronto, Ontario and founded the city's Theatre Resource Centre. Pochinko's technique for which he is known combined both European and First Nations traditions of masked and clown performance.
COACH: Henry Ruttan was a prominent businessman, inventor, and politician in Upper Canada who revolutionized railway travel. In 1858, he patented an innovative system for heating and cooling railway coaches, which was adopted by several railway companies across North America. His system used the motion of the train to force outside air through ducts and a wash tank, where the air was cleaned, humidified, and cooled. During winter, the system was adapted to heat the air entering the cars, making train travel more comfortable year-round. Ruttan’s invention was a game-changer for passenger comfort and a brilliant example of Canadian ingenuity!
COFFEE: September 29th was National Coffee Day! Canadians sure love their coffee - so much that we’re among the top coffee consumers per capita in the world. From bustling cafés in big cities to a double-double at Tims, coffee has become a daily ritual across the country. Whether it’s enjoyed during a crisp autumn walk, a study session, or a cozy chat with friends, a good cup of coffee is a Canadian comfort through and through.
COINS: Canada has some iconic coins, including the $1 loonie and the $2 toonie. DYK: In 2017, the Canadian Mint ran a contest and Canadians chose "Churchill" as the toonie polar bear's official name, a reference both to Winston Churchill and to the common polar bear sightings in Churchill, Manitoba. Canada has even commemorated the coins with monuments: the "Big Loonie" in Echo Bay, Ontario and the "Giant Toonie" in Campbellford, Ontario.
CONTE: Roch Carrier is a French Canadian novelist and author of contes, which are a very brief form of the short story. He is one of Canada's most famous and well-loved authors, and his story "The Hockey Sweater" ("Le chandail de hockey") is an important part of Canadian culture. A quote from the story was even reprinted on the back of the Canadian five-dollar bill.
COOKS: Celebrity Cooks was one of Canada’s first cooking shows, airing from 1975 to 1987 and hosted by Bruno Gerussi of The Beachcombers fame. It mixed celebrity guests with easy, tasty recipes, inspiring a generation of home cooks. Since then, Canadian chefs have kept the country’s culinary scene vibrant, from Stephen Yan of the Canadian-produced Wok with Yan to Chuck Hughes, Lynn Crawford, Mark McEwan, Matty Matheson, Michael Smith, Anna Olson, Susur Lee, and Rob Feenie. These chefs showcase Canada’s diverse culinary talent on TV, in restaurants, and in cookbooks.
COUGH: In 1919, Toronto pharmacist William Knapp Buckley bought a pharmacy and by March of 1920 he had discovered several natural ingredients that had a positive impact on coughs and colds; Buckley's Mixture was born. Buckley's cough syrup is known for its famous campaign slogan: "It tastes awful. And it works."
CRABS: Canada is the largest producer of snow crab in the world, accounting for about two-thirds of the global supply! The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec provide Canada and the world with hundreds of tonnes of snow crab each year. Snow crabs have white flesh with a tinge of pink and a slightly salty flavour offering the perfect balance of sweet and briny.
CRASH: Crash Adams, the Toronto-based pop duo, performed their original song “Optimist” on America’s Got Talent in 2025, earning four “yes” votes from the judges. They were previously nominated for Breakthrough Group of the Year at the 2024 Juno Awards, highlighting their rise in the Canadian music scene. Their energetic blend of pop, rock, and electronic music has won them a devoted fanbase.
CRAVE: Crave is a popular Canadian streaming service offering a wide range of content and programming. Launched by Bell Media in 2014, Crave provides Canadians with access to a rich library of movies, TV shows, and original content. It has become a go-to platform for Canadian viewers craving top-quality entertainment, including hit series like "Game of Thrones," "The Handmaid's Tale," and Canadian originals like "Letterkenny." With its extensive selection and exclusive offerings, Crave has cemented itself as a key player in the Canadian streaming landscape.
CRAWL: Many Canadian kids of the '80s and '90s remember the gentle joy of Fred Penner's Place - and it all began with a crawl! Each episode opened with Fred crawling through a hollow log in the forest, guitar in hand, on his way to a cozy clearing where songs and stories awaited. The show aired on CBC for over a decade, becoming a beloved part of childhood for generations.
CRAZY: "The Crazy Canucks" was the nickname for a group of World Cup alpine ski racers from Canada who rose to prominence in the 1970s and 1980s. Together, Ken Read, Steve Podborski, Dave Irwin and Dave Murray were a cultural phenomenon known as the Crazy Canucks; a team of world class skiers who were the first to challenge the Europeans for downhill supremacy in the sport they’d dominated for decades. "Jungle" Jim Hunter is considered to be the original Crazy Canuck before the core four, and Todd Brooker was the last member of the Crazy Canucks.
CREWS: Paris 2024 will see Canada's first breaking Olympian, as the sport makes its Olympic debut. In breaking, crews are a collective of B-Boys and B-Girls who come together as a team, under one crew name. Being in a crew is an official, important commitment as a crew is a family who train together, battle together, support each other and share the same mindset towards breaking as a dance and culture. Philip Kim, aka B-Boy Phil Wizard, is one of the most creative and original breakers on the hip-hop dance scene and he is representing Canada in Paris 2024!
CRUMB: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert classic from Nanaimo, British Columbia. This no-bake treat has a crumb-based bottom layer made from crushed graham crackers, cocoa, and coconut, topped with a creamy custard icing and finished with a smooth chocolate layer. A perfect blend of textures and flavours, Nanaimo Bars are a sweet Canadian favourite enjoyed across the country!
CUBIC: Canada is one of the world's top producers of diamonds, with mines in the Northwest Territories, Ontario, and Quebec. Diamonds, which are also the birthstone for April, form deep underground in a cubic crystal structure, giving them their signature sparkle! The first Canadian diamond mine, Ekati, opened in the Northwest Territories in 1998, and today, Canada is known for its high-quality, ethically sourced gems.
CURVE: Morant's Curve is a scenic viewpoint near Lake Louise of a dramatic bend along the Bow River where trains pass through the Canadian Rockies. It's a popular viewpoint for photographers in Banff National Park. The iconic Canadian shot that most photographers are looking for is of a beautiful, crimson red train making its way towards the camera through the landscape. The location was named after photographer Nicholas Morant, who was working for the Canadian Pacific Railway in the mid 20th century.
CYBER: Did you know that Canada is a global leader in cybersecurity research and innovation? With the increasing reliance on digital technologies and the internet, cybersecurity has become a critical aspect of protecting individuals, businesses, and governments from cyber threats. In Canada, organizations such as the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange (CCTX) and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) work tirelessly to enhance the nation's cybersecurity posture and collaborate with international partners to address cyber threats.
DELTA: Happy World Rivers Day! Deltas are wetlands that form as rivers empty their water and sediment into another body of water, such as an ocean, lake, or another river. Among the largest deltas in Canada are those of the Mackenzie and Saskatchewan rivers, as well as the Peace-Athabasca Delta. The Mackenzie Delta in Northwest Territories is one of the world's largest river deltas.
DEMON: In 2025, Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters thrilled audiences with a fictional K-Pop girl group battling demons through music. Co-directed by Maggie Kang – born in Seoul, raised in Toronto, and a Sheridan College animation grad – the film blends Korean mythology with Canadian creativity. Its hit song Golden made Billboard history, topping both the Hot 100 and Global 200 charts.
DENIM: The Canadian Tuxedo is an outfit consisting of a denim jacket or jean shirt worn with denim jeans, or denim-on-denim. The term originated in 1951 after Bing Crosby was refused entry to a Vancouver hotel wearing double denim.
DEPOT: In early Canadian history, a depot was more than just a storage spot – it was a lifeline. Trading depots were key hubs during the fur trade era, where Indigenous peoples, voyageurs, and European traders exchanged goods like furs, tools, and textiles. Major depots, such as those run by the Hudson’s Bay Company and North West Company, helped shape trade routes and settlements across Canada. These depots laid the groundwork for many towns and cities we know today!
DERBY: It's the final weekend of the 2023 Calgary Stampede - the world's largest outdoor rodeo! This year, the Stampede is celebrating 100 years of chuckwagon racing at the Cowboys Rangeland Derby! The world’s first Chuckwagon Race was staged at the Calgary Stampede in 1923. A true throwback to the wild west, the event was inspired by the tradition of cowboys breaking camp and racing home. And while some of the rules have since changed, the rush has never left. YAHOO!
DEUCE: In curling, a deuce is when a team scores two points in a single end, giving them a strong advantage on the scoreboard. The new Rock League kicks off in Toronto from April 6-12, featuring an exciting new format and players from across Canada and around the world. With the slogan “Curling Unleashed,” competitors will be sliding, sweeping, and chasing deuces in a week of fast-paced, international curling action.
DOCKS: Across Canada, Victoria Day weekend is widely seen as the unofficial start of summer, and docks across lakes and cottages are finally coming back to life. Millions of Canadians head to cottages or lake regions each year for the May long weekend, making it one of the busiest travel periods of the spring season. Boats return to the water, families gather along shorelines, and communities across the country kick off the season with sunshine, fresh air, and time by the lake.
DOUGH: Today is National Waffle Day! Touton is a traditional dish from Newfoundland produced by frying bread dough on a pan in butter or pork fat. Toutons are often made from leftover bread dough, or dough that was left to rise overnight. This pancake-like dish has emerged as a symbol of Newfoundland identity.
DOWNS: It's Grey Cup Sunday – time for some Canadian football! In the CFL, teams have just three downs to advance the ball ten yards, compared to four in American football. That rule gives the Canadian game its faster pace and wide-open plays. The three-down system has long been a point of pride in Canada, encouraging bold passes, big runs, and thrilling Grey Cup finishes!
DOZEN: Did you know egg cartons were invented by a Canadian? Egg cartons were invented in 1911 in British Columbia by Joseph Coyle after overhearing a dispute over broken eggs between a local farmer and hotel owner. Coyle was a newspaper man and part-time inventor. He designed the very first egg carton from newspaper, with cushioned slots for each egg. The next time your dozen eggs get home safely, make sure to thank Joseph Coyle!
DRAKE: The Village of Andrew, Alberta is home to the world's largest mallard duck! The statue honours the area's wetlands and mallard nesting grounds. It features a male mallard duck (also known as a drake) with a wingspan of 23 feet, weighing 1 tonne and standing seven metres tall. This drake is not quite as famous as Canadian rapper and singer, Drake, who also starred as Jimmy Brooks in the teen drama series Degrassi: The Next Generation.
DRESS: Red Dress Day, also known as the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and Two-Spirit People, is observed annually on May 5th. The day honours and brings awareness to the thousands of Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people who have been subject to disproportionate violence in Canada. Red Dress Day was inspired by Métis artist Jaime Black’s REDress Project installation, in which she hung empty, red dresses to represent the missing and murdered women. Red dresses have become symbolic of the crisis as a result of her installation.
DRIED: Pemmican is a nutrient-rich food made from dried meat, tallow, and sometimes dried berries. Traditionally prepared by Indigenous Peoples in parts of North America, it has long been valued for its long shelf life and high energy content, making it an essential food for survival, particularly during long journeys across Canada's vast landscapes. Pemmican can be eaten raw or used in prepared meals, and it remains part of Indigenous cuisine today. The word pemmican comes from the Cree word 'pimikan,' meaning 'manufactured grease.'
DRUMS: Drumming has always been, and continues to be, an important part of First Nations ceremonies, traditions and cultural practices. Drums are often considered sacred amongst Indigenous peoples, representing the heartbeat of people, animals and Mother Earth herself. Drums range in size from small enough for a child to hold, to large enough to seat several drummers around at a ceremony or powwow.
DUCKS: With roughly 22 different species of duck found in Canada, the most common is the Mallard. Saskatchewan is renowned for having some of the most abundant and productive waterfowl habitat in North America. Check out Ducks Unlimited Canada and how they are working to conserve, restore and manage Canadian wetlands.
EARLY: Natural Resources Canada has developed a national Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) system designed to provide early detection and warning in areas of moderate to high earthquake hazard and with concentrations of population and infrastructure. In Canada, this earthquake risk is concentrated in western British Columbia, eastern Ontario, and southern Quebec. The EEW system began operation in BC in the spring of 2024 and will begin in Quebec and Ontario in early 2025.
EDICT: An edict is a formal announcement or decree that establishes a law or order. Often associated with monarchies, edicts have been used throughout history to communicate official orders, mandates, and laws. In Canada, royal edicts played a key role in shaping governance and establishing provinces under the Crown. The Quebec Act of 1774, an edict from King George III, protected French civil law and religious rights, helping to preserve Quebec's distinct identity. Even today, Canada remains a constitutional monarchy, with royal proclamations continuing to mark significant national events.
EERIE: As Halloween draws near, Canada is home to some truly eerie locations that promise spine-chilling experiences! From the haunted Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta, known for its ghostly bride roaming the halls, to the Ottawa Jail Hostel, where visitors report unsettling encounters, the country offers numerous sites steeped in supernatural lore. These places not only showcase Canada's rich history but also the spooky tales that come alive during the Halloween season. So, if you're in the mood for some thrills this October, consider exploring one of these eerie spots!
EIGHT: Canada has a proud tradition in rowing, especially in the men's and women's eight events. The coxed eight boat class (8 rowers with one oar each and a coxswain to steer) has been Canada's most successful rowing event with notable triumphs on the world stage. The Canadian men's and women's eight teams have collectively won a total of six Olympic medals: two golds and four silvers.
EJECT: The ejection seat, invented in Britain during the 1940s by Sir James Martin of Martin-Baker Aircraft, has saved thousands of pilots’ lives. Canada was among the early adopters, equipping its jets with this life-saving technology. Today, Royal Canadian Air Force pilots flying CF-18 Hornets rely on rocket-powered ejection systems that can launch them clear of danger in under two seconds – a dramatic but vital safeguard in Canadian aviation.
ELBOW: "Elbows Up" is a phrase that means to protect yourself or fight back, and it recently gained attention as Canada flexed its muscle in the ongoing trade dispute with the United States. Just like in hockey, where players use their elbows to shield themselves or push back against opponents, Canada has been using its economic power and strategic policies to stand firm and defend its interests. Whether it's in the rink or the world of international trade, "elbows up" is all about resilience and standing your ground!
ELDER: Elders are respected individuals who play key roles in Indigenous communities. They are important knowledge keepers, and they also help to ensure cultural continuity.
ENDER: Today is Curling Day in Canada! A time to celebrate the great sport of curling and share the benefits of participation with friends, family, and neighbours in communities across the nation. In curling, an 8-ender is an end where all eight stones score for one team; a very rare occurrence. Curling Canada recognizes teams who score 8-enders with pins and certificates.
ENTRY: Entry Island is a small, treeless island off the east coast of Quebec with beautiful rolling green hills, a 1969 lighthouse & a seasonal history museum. It is the only inhabited island of the Magdalen Islands not linked to the archipelago. No matter where you decide to go on this 7.2 km² island, you will be charmed by the beauty of its landscape and its animals living in the wild.
ENVOY: Canada has a proud history of diplomacy and peacekeeping, often playing the role of envoy on the world stage. Canadians have been involved in key international missions as ambassadors, peacekeepers, and negotiators, striving to promote peace and collaboration globally. In fact, Canadian Lester B. Pearson, who served as an envoy in the United Nations, is credited with establishing the modern concept of peacekeeping and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957 for his efforts. Through its envoys, Canada has built a legacy of promoting unity, peace, and goodwill around the world - a true reflection of Canadian values.
EXPAT: Canada is home to a vibrant expat community, with people from around the world making it their home temporarily for work, study, or lifestyle. At the same time, there are over 3 million Canadians living abroad, with popular destinations like the United States, the UK, and Australia. Whether in Canada or overseas, expats play an important role in connecting cultures and expanding global networks.
FAUNA: Canada's fauna is as diverse as its landscapes, from majestic moose roaming the forests and playful otters frolicking in rivers, to bison grazing the plains and beavers diligently building their dams. With over 200 species of mammals, 400 species of birds, and countless other creatures, Canada is a wildlife lover's dream. Whether you're spotting a moose on a forest trail or hearing the call of a loon across a lake, Canada's fauna never fails to leave you in awe.
FENCE: Canadian fencing dates back to 1816 when Maitre Girard opened the first fencing school in Montréal. The first Canadian Championships were held in 1902. The Canadian Fencing Federation was incorporated in 1971 with a mandate is to establish, develop and support fencing in Canada and to represent Canada on the international scene.
FETAL: Montreal born Leon Katz was a pioneering biomedical engineer whose work significantly improved patient care and safety throughout Canada. Katz invented, innovated and hand-crafted a wide range of medical devices: Canada's first fetal heart monitor, a scanner-printer to detect radioactive iodine uptake in the thyroid gland, infant incubators, and a high-speed contrast injector for angiography. Notably, using his own original heart-lung bypass machine, he was the perfusionist for Canada’s first successful open heart surgery, and for thousands of subsequent operations.
FIELD: There are so many different types of fields in Canada: sports fields, wheat fields, oil fields, and ice fields to name a few. The Canadian Prairies are known for their open skies and vast fields of grain, but Canada is also home to the world's largest non-polar ice field in the St. Elias Mountains located in Kluane National Park and Reserve, Yukon Territory.
FIFTH: Canada is home to Baffin Island, the fifth-largest island in the world, located in the Arctic Archipelago. Additionally, Canada's lakes contain one-fifth of the world's fresh water, making the country a key player in the global water supply. From vast landscapes to abundant freshwater, Canada is truly a land of immense natural wonders!
FIFTY: On June 16, 2025, Canadian ultramarathoner and mental health advocate Sachin "Sach" Latti began running 50 km a day for 75 days across Canada, from Victoria, B.C. to St. John’s, Newfoundland. Known as Canada’s Longest Run for Mental Health, his mission aims to raise $1 million for mental health initiatives. Along the way, Sach is connecting with Canadians from all walks of life, sparking open conversations about mental health and inspiring others to take action. You can follow Sach's journey at sachinmotion.ca and support his cross-Canada run with a donation to the Sach In Motion Fund. Every step matters. Every donation helps.
FIGHT: In Canada, fighting stigma around mental health is crucial, and one of the unique initiatives leading the charge is Operation White Heart. Founded in 2022 in Saint John, New Brunswick, this movement encourages people to place a white heart made of garden stones in their yards to show solidarity with those struggling with mental health issues. The initiative aims to spark conversations, remind people they are not alone, and help remove the stigma surrounding mental health and suicide prevention. By simply planting a white heart, individuals are visibly supporting others in their communities, reminding everyone that mental health matters. This simple yet powerful act has spread across the country, making a significant impact on how Canadians approach the topic of mental health.
FINCH: The Fleet Finch is a two-seat, tandem training biplane produced by Fleet Aircraft of Fort Erie, Ontario. Over several years beginning in 1939, a total of 447 Finches were built. The Finch was a mainstay of the Royal Canadian Air Force prior to and during the early part of the Second World War.
FIXER: Property Brothers is a Canadian reality television series that features twin brothers Drew Scott and Jonathan Scott. The Property Brothers help families find, buy, and transform fixer-uppers into dream homes on a strict timeline and budget. The show has aired in over 150 countries around the world!
FJORD: Fjords in Canada are long, narrow inlets characterized by steep sides, created in a valley carved by glacial activity. Canada is home to many of these impressive natural features, including the many islands that make up the Arctic Archipelago in northern Canada, the Saguenay Fjord National Park in Quebec, Newfoundland's iconic Western Brook Pond Fjord located in Gros Morne National Park, and all along the west coast in British Columbia which is one of the longest fjord coastlines in the world!
FLAKE: Edward Anton Maria Asselbergs (1927–1996) was a Dutch-Canadian food chemist famous for inventing the modern process of producing instant mashed potato flakes. He developed the process in 1960 while working for the Canadian Department of Agriculture in Ottawa. The product reached the market in 1962 and it was an instant success!
FLOOD: Flooding stands as Canada's most frequent and expensive natural disaster. In fact, floods account for 40% of weather-related disasters in the country! From spring ice jams in the Red River Valley to coastal storm surges in the Maritimes, flooding can impact communities across the country. Some of Canada's most significant floods include the 2013 Alberta floods, which caused billions in damages, and the 1997 "Flood of the Century" in Manitoba. With climate change increasing extreme weather events, Canada continues to invest in flood prevention to keep communities safe from rising waters.
FLOOR: Samuel Perry Jacks, more commonly known as "Sam Jacks", was a Canadian soldier in World War II, inventor, military and civic recreation director, sports coach, and creator of the Canadian sport of ringette. In 1936, Jacks created the game of floor hockey, and developed the first set of rules, and was recognized by the Youth Branch of the United Nations for the creation of the game.
FLYER: When it made its debut at the 1953 Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, The Flyer roller coaster was the highest and fastest in the world at the time. Its tallest point was 19 m or 62 ft, and it could reach speeds up to 104 km or 65 miles per hour. Two four-car trains sped along the ride's 796 m or 2,612 ft long track for a total of 32 riders per train.
FOODS: McCain Foods is one of Canada’s biggest food success stories, founded in New Brunswick in 1957 and still family-owned today. Best known for its frozen potato products, the company grows and processes potatoes from Canadian farms, helping make fries, hash browns, and many more frozen potato products a staple in freezers across the country. From small-town roots to kitchens around the world, McCain remains proudly Canadian at heart.
FOXES: Four species of foxes live in Canada: arctic, swift, grey, and red being the most common. The grey fox is one of only 2 members of the dog family that can climb trees.
FROST: Canadian winters can be freezing cold. Uncovered skin in freezing temperatures can get frostbite. But that doesn't stop Canadians from having outdoor winter festivals! Frost Regina was just held in Regina, Saskatchewan from Feb 3-12, 2023. This unique city-wide event celebrates the cold winter climate through stunning light installations, local music, captivating art, and rich culture. Frost Regina is where winter comes to life!
FULLY: The Tragically Hip, often referred to simply as the Hip, were a Canadian rock band formed in Kingston, Ontario in 1984, consisting of vocalist Gord Downie, guitarist Paul Langlois, guitarist Rob Baker, bassist Gord Sinclair, and drummer Johnny Fay. They have received numerous Canadian music awards, including 17 Juno Awards. Their album "Fully Completely" is widely considered the Hip's breakthrough record, and songs like "Wheat Kings" and "Courage" became Canadian anthems. The Hip played their final concert together in Kingston on August 20, 2016. Frontman Gord Downie passed away on October 17, 2017 after a battle with brain cancer.
FUNDS: The 45th annual Terry Fox Run invited Canadians to "Finish It", running, walking, or rolling in communities across the country to raise funds for cancer research. Since 1980, participants have raised more than $950 million, keeping Terry’s dream alive and funding breakthroughs that bring hope to millions. Every step, kilometre, and donation helps push the fight against cancer closer to the finish line. You can donate to the Terry Fox Foundation in honour of Terry at terryfox.org.
GAUGE: In Canada, we go big - even when it comes to measuring the wind! In Lethbridge, Alberta, you'll find the world's largest wind gauge, a unique roadside attraction that stands over 17 feet tall. Lethbridge is famous for its strong Chinook winds, so the towering gauge is a fitting tribute to the city's windy reputation. Next time you’re in southern Alberta, check out this quirky Canadian landmark and see if you can "gauge" just how gusty it is!
GEESE: Although Canada has no official bird, the Canada Goose has long been a part of the national identity. Canada Geese are well known for flying in a distinctive V-shaped formation, their loud "honk" and their unmistakable looks.
GENIE: The Genie Awards were given out annually by the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television to recognize the best of Canadian cinema from 1980–2012. The Genie Awards succeeded the Canadian Film Awards (1949-1978), and were merged with the Gemini Awards in 2013 to form the Canadian Screen Awards. The 11th annual Canadian Screen Awards were held at Meridian Hall in Toronto from April 11-14 to honour achievements in Canadian film, television and digital media production. Highlights of the awards ceremony air on CBC and CBC Gem tonight on the final day of Canadian Screen Week 2023!
GENRE: The Juno Awards celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GIVER: The slang word give'r is used in Canada to mean to give it all you've got or to try as hard as possible at something. Also, today is the International Day of Charity! The day was chosen to commemorate the anniversary of the passing away of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her humanitarian work. Canadians are known to be a very generous bunch of givers. In 2021, Canadians gave over $11.8 billion to charitable organizations. Consider donating to your favourite charity today, and just give'r!
GLASS: The Bottle Houses in Cape Egmont, Prince Edward Island was built in 1980 by Édouard Arsenault. It is a must-see tourist attraction that includes life-sized buildings made of over 25,000 recycled coloured glass bottles. The village contains a six-gabled house, a tavern, and a chapel in a tranquil garden setting. The Bottle Houses opens for the 2024 season on May 18th so add it to your summer travel list!
GLAZE: Pottery has been produced by Europeans in Canada since the mid-17th century (and by the Indigenous peoples long before). Glaze is used to give the pottery a glassy coating, for decoration, and to preserve the pottery over time. Today is National Donut Day! To celebrate, Tim Hortons brought back two classic glazed donuts - the Walnut Crunch and the Cherry Stick! We hope you celebrate today with your favourite donut! Our favourite is the Canadian Maple! 🍩🍁
GLIDE: Air Canada Flight 143, commonly known as the Gimli Glider, was a Canadian scheduled domestic passenger flight between Montreal and Edmonton that ran out of fuel on Saturday, July 23, 1983. The flight crew successfully glided the Boeing 767 to an emergency landing at a former Royal Canadian Air Force base in Gimli, Manitoba, which had been converted to a racetrack, Gimli Motorsports Park. It resulted in no serious injuries to passengers or persons on the ground, and only minor damage to the aircraft. This unusual aviation incident earned the aircraft the nickname "Gimli Glider."
GLORY: Glory is what Canadians chase every four years at the Winter Olympics, where unforgettable moments unite the country in celebration. At Vancouver 2010, Canada won 14 gold medals, setting the record for the most golds ever by a host nation. Team Canada continues to shine, chasing sporting glory on the world stage at the 2026 Milano Cortina Games!
GNOME: If you happen to be walking through the Parc écologique Godefroy in Bécancour, Quebec, you might stumble upon a little village complete with tiny houses with working doors and windows, and no shortage of gnomes going about their business. The display, and the handiwork, is straight out of the imagination of Michel Marchand. He built all the little gnome houses himself and crafted the tiny characters who inhabit "Gnome Park" inside the Quebec eco-park. Come walk the paths and discover the magical world of gnomes!
GRAFT: In the Okanagan Valley, renowned for its orchards and vineyards, grafting is a vital horticultural technique. Scion grafting involves joining a young shoot (the scion) from a prized fruit tree onto the rootstock of another, combining strengths to grow healthier, more productive plants. This method helps Okanagan growers cultivate delicious apples, cherries, and grapes suited to the region’s unique climate, supporting one of Canada’s most important fruit-growing areas.
GRANT: The Government of Canada offers funding through grants and contribution (Gs&Cs) programs that help support a variety of jobs, research, training and financial assistance across the country. A grant can provide funding to individuals, nonprofits, community organizations and small businesses to support upcoming projects, programs and initiatives. For many Canadians, the ability to access, stay safe and succeed on the internet is still out of reach. To help close this gap, CIRA is launching its 2024 grants program to support not-for-profits, Indigenous communities, researchers and registered charities across the country that are working to bridge that digital divide. Learn more about CIRA's Net Good Grants program!
GRASS: In Indigenous culture, braided sweet grass is believed to attract good spirits, energies, and influences. Sweet grass, with its sweet aroma reminding people of the love, kindness, and gentleness provided by Mother Earth, is known to have a calming effect and is often used during talking circles and healings. Sweet grass is often used during smudging to call in the good Spirit.
GRAVY: You can't have Canada's national dish without gravy! Poutine (aka "Canadian Salad") is the quintessential Canadian snack of fries and cheese curds covered in gravy.
GREAT: Although it is unknown who coined the term “Great White North” in reference to Canada, the nickname has been in use for many decades. “Great” because it’s the second largest country in the world. “White” because of the amount of Arctic frozen tundra and snow within the country. Finally, “North” because not only does Canada take up most of the northern half of North America, it also stretches nearly to the North Pole! Canada is also home to the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories.
GRIPS: In the sport of wrestling, grips are crucial for securing holds and executing techniques. Canadian wrestlers have excelled in both freestyle and Greco-Roman wrestling, showcasing their mastery of various grips and maneuvers. One notable Canadian wrestler is Erica Wiebe, who won gold in women's freestyle wrestling at the 2016 Rio Olympics. Her incredible performance highlighted the importance of strong grips and technique in achieving success on the mat. Wiebe's victory was a proud moment for Canada, emphasizing the country's strength in wrestling on the world stage and following the Olympic successes of Tonya Verbeek, Carol Huynh, and Daniel Igali.
GROVE: Wander through Vancouver Island's Cathedral Grove in MacMillan Provincial Park and you'll experience the unforgettable sight of some the oldest and tallest trees in Canada. The park's name will make perfect sense when you see sunlight filtering through the soaring 80-metre-high canopy. Plan to spend a few hours wandering Cathedral Grove's trail system and gazing up at 800-year-old giant Douglas Fir, Grand Firs, Western Hemlocks, and Western Red Cedar trees.
GRUNT: If Nova Scotia had an official dessert, it might just be Blueberry Grunt. This timeless combination of wild blueberries and crumbly biscuits is an iconic East Coast classic! This cobbler style dessert is great all year round, but it's best with fresh blueberries in the summer!
GUARD: The Ceremonial Guard is an ad hoc military unit in the Canadian Armed Forces that performs the Changing the Guard ceremony on Parliament Hill and posts sentries at Rideau Hall. We stand on guard for thee!
GUESS: Happy American Thanksgiving! The Guess Who was the most successful Canadian rock group of the late 1960s and early 1970s, and Canada’s first rock superstars. Their impressive catalogue of songs includes "These Eyes," "No Time," and "American Woman" (the first song by a Canadian band to hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart). The Guess Who won two Juno Awards and a Governor General's Performing Arts Award, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, Canada's Walk of Fame, the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Canadian Music Industry Hall of Fame.
GUIDE: Girl Guides of Canada started on September 7, 1910, and Canada was among the founding members of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) in 1928. Some well-known former Girl Guides include: Queen Elizabeth II, Margaret Atwood, Celine Dion, Sarah McLachlan, and Dr. Roberta Bondar, who juggled Girl Guide cookies in space!
GUILD: A guild is an association of artisans and merchants who oversee the practice of their craft/trade in a particular territory. Some notable guilds in Canada include the Canadian Merchant Service Guild, Canadian Media Guild, Writers Guild, Directors Guild, Playwrights Guild, Screen Composers Guild, and various Quilters, Spinners & Weavers Guilds!
HAIRY: It’s the end of Movember, and things got a little hairy across Canada this past month! From handlebar to horseshoe, moustaches of every style helped raise awareness and funds for men’s health, supporting research and programs for prostate cancer, testicular cancer, mental health, and suicide prevention. Canuckle co-creators Mark and Jeff proudly joined the cause – growing their own Mo’s to spark conversation and support this important movement. Thanks to all the hairy heroes across the country who helped make a difference this Movember!
HAUNT: Halloween Haunt is on right now at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto! Halloween Haunt turns the theme park into a scream park filled with Halloween attractions that offer unforgettable thrills and unspeakable horror. From rides, to scare zones, to monsters, it's Canada's biggest haunted wonderland! So, whether you’re seeking heart-pounding coaster thrills or spine-tingling scares, Canada’s Wonderland Halloween Haunt has it all.
HAWKS: The Golden Hawks were a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aerobatic flying team established in 1959 to celebrate the 35th anniversary of the RCAF and the "Golden" 50th anniversary of Canadian flight, which began with the AEA Silver Dart in 1909.
HELLO: Happy Victoria Day! 👑 Hello! Canada magazine is a Canadian entertainment magazine that launched in 2006 by Rogers Media. Published weekly, it covers the latest celebrity and royal news from around the world. Hello! Canada has become a beloved publication among Canadian readers, so much so that it is the top-selling magazine on Canadian newsstands and is a leading entertainment brand online!
HILLS: On Vimy Ridge Day, we remember the bravery of Canadian soldiers who fought in one of the most pivotal battles of World War I. The rugged hills of Vimy Ridge posed a massive challenge, as soldiers had to climb and fight through difficult terrain to capture the position from enemy forces. The victory at Vimy in 1917 marked a defining moment in Canadian history, solidifying Canada's reputation on the world stage. Today, the Vimy Memorial stands proudly on those very hills, honouring the sacrifices of those who fought there.
HOIST: Today is National Flag Day! When it comes to flags, the hoist is the part of the flag closest to the flagpole. On February 15, 1965, the new National Flag of Canada was officially hoisted for the first time on Parliament Hill. As the flag was raised, it symbolized a new chapter in Canada's history. With its bold red and white maple leaf design, the flag quickly became a unifying symbol of national pride. As we celebrate 60 years of this iconic emblem, Canadians continue to hoist their flag high with pride from coast to coast to coast.
HOLLY: Holly, a symbol of holiday cheer, adds a beautiful touch to Canadian winter decor with its glossy green leaves and bright red berries. Though not native to Canada, English and American holly thrive in British Columbia, especially around Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland, where the mild climate supports their growth. In Newfoundland and Labrador, there's even a native type called Mountain holly, adding a uniquely Canadian twist to this festive plant. From wreaths to garlands, holly's vibrant colours bring warmth to Canadian homes and holiday traditions coast to coast.
HONEY: Canadian honey is recognized around the world for its high quality. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta produce 80% of Canada's honey crop. Canada is the world's sixth largest producer of honey. The average honey yield per hive in Canada is twice the world's average due to our long and warm summer days and a vast supply of nectar producing crops!
HURON: With the longest shoreline of all of the Great Lakes, Lake Huron is one of the most unique lakes on Earth. It is the second largest of the Great Lakes, and the fourth largest lake in the world by surface area. The Huron Wendat are an Iroquoian-speaking nation in Canada, originally living along the St. Lawrence River and between Lake Huron and Lake Ontario.
HURRY: In Canada, "hurry hard" is curling’s battle cry, as team members sweep harder and faster. Hurry Hard is such an iconic phrase that it was the title for Canadian curling legend Russ Howard's memoir, it was the name of a curling comedy show put on by the Playgoers of Lethbridge, and it was enshrined as the name of an amber lager beer by Toronto's Triple Bogey Brewing Company. Tune in to the 2024 World Women's Curling Championship this week in Sydney, Nova Scotia where you'll be sure to hear a few "Hurry Hard" calls from Rachel Homan who is wearing the maple leaf as Team Canada!
HYDRO: Waterpower is Canada's most abundant source of clean and renewable electricity, providing more than 60% of Canada's total electricity today. Canada is the fourth largest generator of hydroelectricity in the world.
IGLOO: Igloo comes from the Inkuktitut word “iglu” meaning house.
INDEX: The S&P/TSX Composite Index has provided investors with a premier indicator of market activity for Canadian equity markets since its launch in 1977. With approximately 95% coverage of the Canadian equities market, it is the primary gauge for Canadian-based, TSX-listed companies.
INLAY: Inlay artwork is a decorative technique that embeds one material within another to create patterns or designs. Indigenous artists in Canada have long used inlay to add meaning and beauty to their work, incorporating materials like shell, bone, stone, or metal into wood and other surfaces. The technique appears in carvings, tools, ceremonial objects, and jewelry, with patterns that often reflect stories, symbols, and connections to the land.
IVORY: International Inuit Day on November 7 celebrates the rich cultural heritage of Inuit communities across Canada's Arctic, including their incredible craftsmanship. Among their many innovations, Inuit carvers have long used natural materials like ivory to craft intricate art pieces and practical tools. Traditional Inuit snow goggles (Inuktitut: ilgaak or iggaak), often made from ivory or bone, were designed with narrow slits to protect against the bright Arctic sun reflecting off the snow - an innovative design to prevent snow blindness.
JAZZY: Canada is home to numerous jazz festivals each year, including the Festival International de Jazz de Montréal (FIJM) which attracts over 2 million visitors annually and is recognized by Guinness World Records as the largest jazz festival on the planet. A number of Canadian jazz artists have achieved international prominence, including Oscar Peterson, Maynard Ferguson, Gil Evans, and Diana Krall.
JEEPS: Did you know that Canada played a significant role in the production of military jeeps during World War II? The Willys MB, commonly known as the 'jeep,' was a versatile vehicle used by Allied forces for various military purposes, including transportation, reconnaissance, and even combat. Canadian factories, such as the Ford Motor Company of Canada in Windsor, Ontario, were instrumental in manufacturing these iconic vehicles to support the war effort. In fact, Canada produced over 100,000 military jeeps during the war, contributing to the Allied victory. Today, the jeep remains a symbol of Canadian wartime manufacturing prowess and innovation.
JELLO: Did you know that Jell-O has a sweet connection to Canada? In the 1930s and '40s, the iconic wobbly dessert became a pantry staple across the country thanks to clever advertising on Canadian radio and in magazines. Starting in 1906, jello was produced in Fort Erie, Ontario, and later in Cobourg, helping supply sweet, jiggly treats to Canadians coast to coast. From strawberry to lime, those colourful cubes became a fixture at church potlucks, school lunches, and yes, even hospital trays. Whether you slurped it, sliced it, or layered it in a retro salad, Jell-O has long had a place in Canadian kitchens!
JEWEL: Looking for the biggest jewel in Canada? The town of Black Diamond, Alberta, is home to the world's largest black diamond! This striking monument was unveiled during the town's centennial Jubilee in 2007, paying homage to its namesake and rich coal mining history. Standing 1.22 metres wide and crafted from painted aluminum, the diamond is more than just a dazzling sight - it symbolizes the resilience and ingenuity of the community that once thrived on coal mining. On January 1, 2023, Black Diamond took on a new chapter in its history by amalgamating with its neighbour, Turner Valley, to form the town of Diamond Valley. Today, Diamond Valley is celebrated not only for its jewel, but also for its vibrant arts scene and stunning foothills views, making it a true gem of Alberta!
JIFFY: Jiffy, Canada's #1 home maintenance app, has been revolutionizing how Canadians tackle their home maintenance since its launch in Toronto in 2015. The app connects homeowners with vetted local service professionals across over 20 categories, such as plumbing, electrical work, and painting. Its name reflects its core promise: connecting users with reliable pros in a jiffy! Since its inception, Jiffy has completed over 450,000 jobs and expanded to cities like Ottawa and Calgary. This homegrown innovation has made managing home repairs easier from coast to coast!
JOLLY: Toronto mother Susan Olivia Poole was an Indigenous Canadian inventor who invented the Jolly Jumper after her first child was born in 1910. In 1948 they were produced for the retail market, and by 1957, the Jolly Jumper was patented.
JUDGE: The Supreme Court of Canada consists of nine judges, including the Chief Justice of Canada, who are appointed by the Governor in Council. The current Chief Justice is Richard Wagner, who succeeded the longest-serving Chief Justice in Canadian history and the first woman to hold the position - Beverley McLachlin.
JUMPS: In Canada, trampolining isn't just a hobby – it's a celebrated sport that takes leaps and bounds to new heights! Canadian athletes have excelled in this dynamic sport, with trampoline gymnastics becoming an Olympic event in 2000. Canadian trampoline gymnast Rosie MacLennan won back-to-back gold medals in 2012 and 2016, making her the only trampolinist to defend her Olympic title successfully.
JUROR: In Canada, each of us has a part in ensuring that the law works properly and that justice is done. Serving on a jury is one way a citizen can carry out their role. In Canada, a criminal law jury is made up of 12 jurors selected from among citizens of the province or territory in which the court is located. It is the civic duty of all Canadian citizens 18 years of age and older to serve as a juror if selected.
KAYAK: Kayaks were originally designed for hunting and fishing. In fact, the word kayak means “hunter's boat”, and came from “qajaq” or “qayarq”, a Greenlandic Inuit word.
KINGS: Today is Commonwealth Day! The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
KIOSK: If you’ve flown internationally into Canada, you’ve likely used a CBSA Primary Inspection Kiosk! Operated by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), which oversees border management and security, these kiosks have streamlined the arrival process since their introduction in 2017. Travellers can scan their passports, snap a quick photo, and complete their customs declarations digitally. Found in major airports across Canada, they help reduce wait times and enhance efficiency while maintaining Canada’s high standards for border security.
KITTY: During the Klondike Gold Rush, Kathleen "Klondike Kate" Rockwell, affectionately known as "Kitty," became one of the Yukon's most celebrated entertainers. Drawn by tales of fortune, Kitty arrived in Dawson City in 1900 and quickly found fame as a dancer. She dazzled packed saloons with her vaudeville routines, including her signature "Flame Dance," which transformed her red sequined dress and flowing chiffon into a fiery spectacle.
