A symbol of resilience and charm, Kitty brought joy and excitement to the often grueling lives of miners who had flocked to the north in search of gold. Kitty's name remains synonymous with the Klondike spirit, capturing the allure and larger-than-life characters that defined one of Canada's most legendary eras.
KUDOS: On Canadian Armed Forces Day, Canadians offer kudos to the women and men of the Canadian Armed Forces, past and present, for their courage, selflessness, and service to Canada at home and abroad. Observed on the first Sunday in June, the day recognizes members of the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force, along with the families who support them in their commitment to stand on guard for Canada. It is a time to reflect, remember, and say thank you.
LEARN: October 5 is World Teachers’ Day, a time to celebrate the educators who inspire students to learn and grow. Across Canada, more than 500,000 teachers bring creativity, dedication, and heart into their classrooms each day. Their efforts are a big reason why Canada is recognized for its strong public education system, consistently ranking among the best in the world. Thank you to all the teachers who make a difference every day!
LILAC: Lilacs are a spring flower and you can find these in gardens across Canada, but the small village of Franktown, Ontario, part of the township of Beckwith, is special as it is known as the Lilac Capital of Ontario. This Lanark County township near Ottawa is famous for its country road called Lilac Lane bordered by beautiful, fragrant lilac bushes, and is home to an annual Lilac Festival every May. If you love gardens, add the Franktown Lilac Festival to your travel list.
LIMIT: Did you know that in Canada, even your change has a limit? Under the Currency Act, there are caps on how much you can use in coins for one purchase: up to $25 in loonies, $40 in toonies, $10 in dimes, $10 in quarters, and just $5 in nickels. These limits exist to stop “coin overload” at the counter – so while a store can accept more, they don’t have to once those limits are reached. So next time, leave the big bag of loonies and toonies at home!
LINGO: Before Canuckle brought daily word fun to Canadians, there was Lingo – the classic word game show that combined luck, logic, and quick thinking! Produced in Vancouver and originally airing in the late 1980s, Lingo featured contestants guessing five-letter words to fill a bingo-style grid, with each correct guess bringing them closer to a winning line. A Canadian version later aired in the late 1990s, hosted by Paul Houde, introducing a new generation to the fun of wordplay. Decades later, Canadians are still hooked on guessing words – proving that a love for lingo never goes out of style!
LINKS: The Perth Golf Course, formally the Links O'Tay Golf & Country Club, located in Perth, Ontario is the oldest golf course in Canada to remain in continous play on the same site. The original three-hole course was designed and put in play in 1890 by Captain A.C. Matheson on a portion of his pasture land located beside the Tay River. Golf quickly gained popularity in the area and the course was soon expanded to 9 holes.
LITRE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and litre is the standard spelling of the metric unit for liquid volume. Canadians purchase gasoline in litres, and also buy milk by the litre (in bags in parts of Ontario, Quebec, and the Maritimes!).
LODGE: A beaver home is called a lodge. Beavers live in wetland habitats along lakes and rivers and are some of the best architects in the wild. Some even call them the original Canadian lumberjacks!
LOGIC: Happy Star Trek Day! In the Star Trek universe, Vulcans are an extraterrestrial humanoid species known as logical beings who have removed emotions from their daily lives. The official Star Trek Capital of Canada is Vulcan, Alberta. The town even has a prominent display of a Starship Enterprise statue. Live long and prosper! 🖖
LOOSE: In Calgary, Alberta, you’ll find a legendary spot for improv comedy called the Loose Moose Theatre, a Canadian institution since 1977! Famous for its hilarious, off-the-cuff performances, Loose Moose has launched the careers of many comedians and actors, and it remains a beloved venue for improv lovers. If you ever feel like laughing 'til you’re loose from your seat, this is the place to be. Plus, it’s all proudly Canadian - combining creativity, humour, and a bit of wild fun, just like the theatre’s name suggests!
LUCKY: Whenever Canada needs a bit of good fortune at the Olympic Games, you can count on a lucky loonie to come through. The tradition was started in 2002 at the Salt Lake City Olympics when Canadian icemaker Trent Evans snuck a loonie underneath centre ice when needing a marker for the faceoff dot. Evans left the loonie there as a good luck charm for the Canadians, and it worked beautifully, with Canada winning gold in both men's and women's hockey for the first time.
LUNAR: Happy Lunar New Year! The Lunar New Year is an event celebrated by millions of people across the world on the first new moon of their calendar. It marks the beginning of the new year based on the lunar calendar or lunisolar calendar. It is one of the largest celebrations for Canada's Chinese population, and it is also celebrated by Canadians from Vietnam, Korea and Southeast Asia, among others.
LYRIC: The Lyric Theatre is a performing arts theatre located in Swift Current, Saskatchewan. The building was declared a municipal heritage property in 2007. The theatre was originally built as a Vaudeville and silent film theatre with 400 seats. From 1918 to 1981, the theatre was operated as a movie theatre, but throughout its history has hosted a variety of events including orchestras, lectures, balls, church services, pet and poultry shows and dance classes, as well as serving as makeshift isolation quarters during the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918.
MAGIC: The International Brotherhood of Magicians (I.B.M.) is an organization for both professional and amateur close-up and stage magicians, with approximately 15,000 members worldwide. It was founded in Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1922, and is now the largest organization of magicians in the world. Winnipeg was also home to one of Canada's most famous magicians, Doug Henning, who had a storied career around the world. He retired in the mid-1980s, selling some of his most famous illusions to another famous magician, David Copperfield.
MAIZE: Did you know that maize, or corn, is one of Canada's most important crops? It thrives particularly in Ontario and Quebec, where it’s often used for animal feed, as well as human consumption in products like corn syrup and popcorn. As Halloween approaches, corn becomes a festive staple, with many Canadians decorating their homes with corn husks and using maize to create seasonal decorations like cornucopias or even haunted corn mazes. These maize mazes offer a fun way for families to celebrate the spooky season while appreciating the agricultural heritage of Canada.
MASKS: Today marks the start of the 2023-24 National Hockey League Season! The goaltender mask is now a mandatory piece of equipment, but that wasn't always the case. The first goaltender to wear a mask in any level of organized ice hockey was Elizabeth Graham of Queen’s University in 1927 who wore a fencing mask. The first NHL goalie to wear a mask full-time was Jacques Plante of the Montreal Canadiens. During the 1959 season, Plante wore a face-hugging fibreglass mask created by Bill Burchmore, a children’s hockey coach and Canadiens fan who worked at Fiberglas Canada in Montreal. Goalie masks have certainly come a long way since then!
MEDIC: Jennie Trout became Canada’s first licensed female physician in 1875 when she received her medical licence from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario. As a trailblazing medic, she challenged 19th-century norms and opened doors for women in medicine. Trout went on to establish a successful practice in Toronto, inspiring countless women to follow in her footsteps. Her legacy remains a milestone in Canadian healthcare history.
MERIT: Established by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II on 1 July 1972, the Order of Military Merit (ORMM) recognizes distinctive merit and exceptional service displayed by the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces. It is the second highest order administered by the governor in Council, on behalf of the Canadian monarch. More than 5,000 members of the Canadian Armed Forces have been appointed to the Order since its creation.
MERRY: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! Across Canada, "Merry Christmas" rings out as part of holiday traditions from coast to coast. While customs vary by region, the season brings a shared spirit of joy and warmth throughout the country. Canadians celebrate with everything from festive parades to bustling holiday markets, gathering with family, friends, and neighbours to make the season special. Whether it's around a Christmas tree, at an outdoor rink, or in a snowy winter wonderland, Canada's holiday spirit is as bright and cheerful as the greeting itself!
MILES: Before Canada adopted the metric system in the 1970s, distances were measured in miles - a reminder of which still lingers in some old road signs and stories! One stunning place that shares the name is Miles Canyon near Whitehorse, Yukon. Once a major hazard for Klondike Gold Rush stampeders navigating the Yukon River, this dramatic canyon features striking basalt cliffs formed by ancient lava flows and stunning emerald-green waters rushing beneath.
MINER: Happy National Mining Week! Canada has a rich history of mining, with numerous communities across the country built on the back of the mining industry. One such community is Estevan, Saskatchewan, known for its coal mining heritage and the iconic character 'Lignite Louie.' Lignite Louie, a fictional character created by the local mining industry, symbolizes the hardworking spirit and resilience of the miners who toiled underground to extract lignite coal, a type of low-grade coal found in the region. Estevan's coal mines played a vital role in powering Saskatchewan's economy and providing employment opportunities for generations of miners and their families. The next time you hear about a miner in Canada, remember the hardworking men and women who helped build the nation's mining industry and shaped the communities we know today.
MINES: In 2020, Canada produced 60 minerals and metals at almost 200 mines, and the value of Canada's mineral production reached $43.8 billion.
MOCHA: Happy National Coffee Day! A caffè mocha is a chocolatey twist on a latte – made with espresso, steamed milk, and chocolate. It’s also known as a Mocaccino or Mochaccino, and Canadian coffee shops like Second Cup Café serve their own take on this sweet favourite. Canadians are passionate about their coffee, with 71% drinking it regularly – more than tap water! Whether you enjoy it hot or iced, a mocha is a perfect way to celebrate the day with a cozy Canadian cup.
MODAL: Modal is a soft, breathable fabric made from beech-tree pulp, prized for its comfort, flexibility, and durability. In Canada, Montreal-based company Manmade uses modal to make everyday essentials like boxer briefs and t-shirts, combining comfort with thoughtful design. Their innovative approach even earned them a deal on Dragon’s Den, helping the company grow into a true Canadian success story and proving that smart ideas and quality materials can take Canadian brands to the next level.
MOGUL: Canadian moguls skiers have won an impressive 9 Olympic medals over the years! Medallists include Jean-Luc Brassard, Jennifer Heil, Alexandre Bilodeau, sisters Justine & Chloé Dufour-Lapointe, and Mikaël Kingsbury. Bilodeau won a gold medal in the men's moguls at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, becoming the first Canadian to win a gold medal at an Olympic Games held in Canada.
MONEY: People from around the world refer to Canadian Money as "rainbow money" or "Monopoly money" thanks to its bright colours and unique artwork.
MOOSE: The moose is the largest species of deer in the world. The average weight of a fully grown male moose (a bull) is 1500 lbs!
MOTTO: The motto of Canada is "A Mari Usque Ad Mare", which translates to "From Sea to Sea". The motto was first officially used in 1906 on the head of the mace of the new Legislative Assembly of Saskatchewan. As part of the Canadian coat of arms, the motto is used as a mark of authority by various government agencies and representatives. It is also present on all denominations of Canadian banknotes, and on the cover of Canadian passports.
MOUND: The Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung Historical Centre, or Manitou Mounds, is Canada's premier concentration of ancient burial mounds. Manitou Mounds National Historic Site, as it was once called, is a vast network of 30 village sites and 15 ancient burial mounds constructed from approximately 5000 BP during the Archaic Period, to 360 BP. It is one of the "most significant centres of early habitation and ceremonial burial in Canada."
MUDDY: The Big Muddy Badlands in southwestern Saskatchewan are a breathtaking mix of rugged beauty and rich history. Nestled within the Big Muddy Valley, this unique landscape features striking cliffs, hoodoos, and winding trails shaped by millennia of erosion. At the heart of the region lies Big Muddy Lake, a shallow, picturesque body of water that complements the area's stark, otherworldly charm. This hidden gem offers visitors a chance to explore Saskatchewan’s dramatic geography and learn about the deep cultural significance of the land to Indigenous peoples. It's a truly muddy marvel waiting to be discovered!
MUMMY: As spooky season is upon us, let's talk about a famous "mummy" of sorts in Dawson City, Yukon! The legendary Sourtoe Cocktail involves a mummified human toe, which is dropped into a drink. Participants who are brave enough take a sip with the preserved toe touching their lips, all in the spirit of a tradition that dates back to the 1970s. While it’s not your typical Halloween mummy, it’s certainly a Canadian story that’s both eerie and fascinating!
MURAL: The world's tallest mural can be found in downtown Calgary, Alberta! It was completed in the summer of 2022 by internationally renowned graffiti artist Mirko Reisser (known as DAIM) and stands 95 metres high on the side of a building across the train tracks from the Calgary Tower. It took 130 litres of paint primer, 207 litres of base coat paint and 543 cans of spray paint.
MUSIC: The Canadian music industry is the sixth-largest in the world, producing internationally renowned composers, musicians and ensembles. O Canada!
NAKED: Did you know Canada is home to some famous nude beaches, like Vancouver's Wreck Beach, one of the largest in North America? Not only do Canadians have a reputation for embracing natural beauty, but we’ve also got "naked" talent in our music scene! From the bold and fearless rocker Bif Naked, to the fun and quirky Barenaked Ladies, Canadian culture has a knack for celebrating individuality. So whether you're enjoying nature or jamming out, there's always a place for "naked" fun in Canada!
NATAL: In Nova Scotia, Natal Day is celebrated on the first Monday in August and marks the "birth" of the Halifax–Dartmouth area. The name comes from the Latin natalis, meaning birth – fitting for a holiday that honours the founding of Halifax in 1749 and the growth of neighbouring communities. First celebrated in 1895, Natal Day has grown into a beloved long weekend tradition filled with parades, fireworks, concerts, and one of Canada’s oldest road races. It’s a joyful celebration of Nova Scotia’s history and coastal spirit!
NEVER: Never Cry Wolf by Canadian author Farley Mowat is a landmark work of Canadian nature writing that follows his time studying Arctic wolves in the North. First published in 1963, the book challenged widespread fears about wolves and helped shift public perception toward understanding and conservation. Blending observation, storytelling, and humour, it remains one of Canada’s most influential wilderness narratives.
NICKEL: Canada has a long history with nickel, so much so that our five-cent coin earned its name from the metal! The town of Sudbury, Ontario became one of the world’s leading sources of nickel after a massive deposit was discovered in the late 1800s—thanks to a meteor strike over 1.8 billion years ago! To celebrate this mining heritage, Sudbury is home to the Big Nickel, a 9-metre-tall replica of a 1951 Canadian nickel. It’s one of Canada’s most iconic roadside attractions!
NIGHT: Hockey Night in Canada (HNIC) is a weekly Saturday night broadcast of NHL games. It has been a staple in Canadian homes since the first radio broadcast in 1931. HNIC began airing on Saturday nights on CBC Television in 1952. It is Canada’s longest-running television program and the Guinness World Record holder as the longest-running TV sports program. Instant replay even made its world debut on a 1955 Hockey Night in Canada broadcast.
NINJA: The Canadian Ninja League is a competition that features obstacle courses inspired by the popular television show American Ninja Warrior(™). Across Canada, Ninja gyms host regional competitions through-out the year where participants compete in various stages of challenging obstacles to demonstrate their speed, strength, and agility. The Canadian Ninja League National Finals are in Edmonton Nov 24-26, 2023!
NINTH: Did you know that the border between Canada and the United States along the 49th parallel is the longest undefended international boundary in the world? Stretching over 8,891 kilometres, the 49th parallel serves as the dividing line between the two countries for much of their shared border. The bi-national International Boundary Commission deals with matters relating to marking and maintaining the boundary, and the International Joint Commission deals with issues concerning boundary waters.
NORDIC: Nordic climates are defined by long, cold winters – something much of Canada knows well, with average February temperatures below freezing across most of the country. Those conditions have helped shape Canada’s strength in Nordic sports like cross-country skiing, ski jumping, biathlon, and Nordic combined, where athletes train for endurance, precision, and resilience in the cold. With the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milano–Cortina starting on February 6, many of Canada’s Nordic athletes will once again put those winter-hardened skills to the test on the world stage.
NOVEL: Canadian authors have given the world some outstanding must read novels, including "The Handmaid's Tale" by Margaret Atwood, "The Book of Negroes" by Lawrence Hill, "Indian Horse" by Richard Wagamese, "Anne of Green Gables" by Lucy Maud Montgomery, "Life of Pi" by Yann Martel, and "Five Little Indians" by Michelle Good, just to name a few. Canadian literature has certainly made its mark!
NURSE: Happy National Nursing Week! Annual celebrations take place in Canada from the Monday to the Sunday of the same week as Florence Nightingale’s birthday on May 12. The week draws attention to nurses, increasing the awareness of the many contributions of nursing to the well-being of Canadians. The first integrated nursing degree program in Canada was started at the University of Toronto in 1942. Today, Canada is one of the few countries in the world requiring a bachelor’s degree for entry to practice as a registered nurse (RN). In 2021, there were 312,382 RNs licensed to practise in Canada. Thank you to all the nurses for everything you do!
NYMPH: In Canada’s cold freshwater ecosystems, including trout streams in the Rockies, many insects such as mayflies and dragonflies spend the early part of their lives as aquatic nymphs. These underwater stages can last from months to years as they develop in rivers and lakes. Mayfly nymphs are especially important in the food chain, serving as a key food source for native trout and other freshwater fish across Canada.
ONION: The onion is Canada's most important condiment crop. It is a biennial, herbaceous plant of the Amaryllidaceae family. In 2022, the annual Canadian production of dry onions was over 287,000 metric tons, worth approximately $157.2 million. Dry onions are mainly produced in Quebec (46%), Ontario (37%) and Alberta (10%). There is even a species of onion called the Canada onion (Allium canadense) that is native to eastern North America.
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORDER: The Order of Canada is how our country honours people who make extraordinary contributions to the nation.
ORGAN: Canadian Joseph Casavant was a world-renowned organ maker. In 1840, he produced his first church organ in his shop at Saint-Hyacinthe. When he retired in 1866, Casavant organs were in demand throughout eastern Canada. Under the direction of his sons, Claver and Samuel, the firm Casavant Frères acquired an international reputation as builders of fine instruments. Casavant Frères continues to build internationally recognized pipe organs for churches, concert halls, religious communities and teaching institutions.
OTTER: Canada is home to both river otters and sea otters. While river otters can be found in every province and territory, sea otters are mainly found on Canada's west coast. Scientists consider the sea otter to be a keystone species - one that modifies and creates its habitat. When it was gone from Canadian waters, kelp forests declined because urchins and other animals that eat seaweed weren't controlled by the otter preying on them. With the return of the otter, kelp forests are in much better shape. This is important because healthy kelp forests provide habitat to fish and reduce coastal erosion by slowing water currents. Sea otters are also of some importance to West Coast Indigenous Peoples - they are depicted in their art and featured in their stories.
OUTER: The vastness of outer space is now a little more Canadian! As the Artemis II crew completes its historic lunar flyby mission, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen is aboard the Orion spacecraft, travelling over 400,000 kilometres from Earth. Hansen is the first Canadian to journey this far into outer space, taking part in humanity’s first trip around the Moon in over half a century.
OWNER: Happy Canadian Innovation Week! Business owners are the backbone of the Canadian economy, with small and medium-sized enterprises making up a whopping 99.8% of all businesses in the country. From local coffee shop owners to cutting-edge tech start-ups, these entrepreneurs drive growth and spark innovation across the nation. With their strong entrepreneurial spirit, Canadian business owners are fuelling progress, creating jobs, and helping communities thrive from coast to coast to coast.
PAGER: The telephone pager was invented in 1949 by Canadian Alfred J. Gross, a Toronto-based wireless communications pioneer. The devices Alfred invented also led to cordless and cellular telephone technology.
PAINT: Norman Breakey from Toronto created the first paint roller in 1939. Unfortunately, he didn't patent the innovation and knock-offs quickly emerged. He may not get the credit he deserves, but Norman's invention has aided generations of painters. Next time you are painting a wall or ceiling, take a moment to remember Canadian Norman Breakey!
PANSY: The pansy is a hardy, colourful flower that has been a favourite in Canadian gardens for generations. Known for its distinctive “face-like” petals, it thrives in cooler climates, making it perfect for parks, public gardens, and window boxes from British Columbia to Newfoundland. In Canada, pansies are often planted in spring and fall, adding bright, cheerful colours even when temperatures dip.
PARKA: Originally created by the Inuit to keep warm in the Canadian Arctic, the first parkas were made from whale, seal or caribou skin and often coated with fish oil for waterproofing.
PATIO: Happy Victoria Day! Today is a federal Canadian public holiday celebrated annually on the last Monday preceding May 25 to honour Queen Victoria. The holiday has been observed in Canada since at least 1845, originally on Victoria's natural birthday, May 24. Today also marks the unofficial start to the summer season in Canada, and along with the warmer weather comes patio season! However you celebrate this long weekend, we hope you get to enjoy some beautiful weather on a patio and support local businesses!
PENCE: Issued in 1851, the 'Three-Pence Beaver' stamp is considered one of the most iconic and sought-after stamps in Canadian philatelic history. The stamp depicted a beaver, a symbol of Canada's fur trade and natural heritage. At the time of its issuance, Canada was still using the British currency system, which included pence, shillings, and pounds. The stamp marked a significant milestone in Canada's postal history, as it was the first adhesive postage stamp issued by the Province of Canada, which later became the Dominion of Canada in 1867.
PENNY: Penny Oleksiak made history by becoming Canada's most decorated Olympian, bringing home multiple medals in swimming from the 2016 and 2020 Olympics. Meanwhile, the Canadian penny, once a staple in our pockets, was discontinued in 2013 due to the cost of production outweighing its value. Although the penny is no longer used in daily transactions, it remains a cherished part of Canadian history and many people still keep them as mementos. The penny may be out of circulation, but Penny Oleksiak continues to shine as a symbol of Canadian excellence on the world stage!
PEONY: Peonies are a beloved flower in Canadian gardens, known for their vibrant blooms and resilience to our northern climate. The Canadian Peony Society, established in 1998, is dedicated to the cultivation and appreciation of these beautiful flowers. Peonies are often seen as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune in many cultures, and their lush blossoms make them a popular choice for Canadian gardens. With over 30 species of peonies found worldwide, they thrive in Canada's diverse climates from coast to coast!
PHONE: In 1876, Scottish-born inventor Alexander Graham Bell patented the first practical telephone, a concept that he conceived in Brantford, Ontario.
PIECE: Towering over the Guinness-certified World’s Largest Chess Set in Medicine Hat, Alberta between the library and the Court of King’s Bench is what could be the World’s Largest Chess Piece. Installed in 2021, the king piece stands 20 feet, 11 inches (6.37m) tall and is 9 feet, 3 inches (2.81m) at the base. The current record-holding piece is in St. Louis, standing 20 feet (6.09m) tall and 9 feet, 2 inches (2.79m) at the base. The Medicine Hat Chess Club will be in contact with Guinness World Records to see if there’s a new king in town.
PILOT: One of Canada's most famous pilots, Billy Bishop was a Canadian flying ace of the First World War. He was officially credited with 72 victories, making him the top Canadian and British Empire ace of the war. The Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport was named in his honour. Today would have been Billy Bishop's 129th birthday!
PINTS: On October 9th, Canadians across the country raise their glasses to celebrate Canadian Beer Day, a day dedicated to the craft, culture, and community that beer fosters from coast to coast. With over 85% of the beer consumed in Canada brewed locally, our pints tell a story of connection, pride, and homegrown flavour. Whether you're enjoying a cold one at a local brewery or sharing a laugh over a pint with friends, Canadian beer brings us together. Cheers to community and great Canadian beer!
PIVOT: Burdett, Alberta is home to the first pivot irrigation system in Canada. The first water drive pivot irrigation system was introduced to Canada by Donald and Wyman Campbell, who moved to the area from Nebraska during 1962. The system was in operation by May 1962 and was used continuously for 25 years.
PIXEL: IMAX, the groundbreaking cinematic format known for its jaw-dropping visuals, was proudly invented in Canada! Developed by Graeme Ferguson and his team in the 1960s, IMAX changed the movie experience forever – first with giant film reels, and now with advanced digital projection powered by millions of pixels. Each pixel helps create the stunning clarity and immersive scale that make IMAX unlike anything else. From its roots at home to theatres around the globe, it’s a pixel-powered breakthrough showcasing Canadian innovation!
PIXIE: Canada's forests are home to the enchanting pixie cup lichen, a tiny, moss-like species that adds a touch of whimsy to the landscape! These small, cup-shaped lichens - named for their resemblance to a pixie's drinking cup - can be found on decaying wood and forest floors across Canada. More than just cute, pixie cup lichen plays a key role in forest ecosystems, helping to break down organic matter and even absorb pollutants. Keep an eye out for these little wonders next time you're exploring a Canadian forest!
PIZZA: Pizza is one of the most popular foods in the world, and Canada is no exception. There is even “Canadian pizza” which typically includes tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, bacon, pepperoni, and mushrooms. The country's biggest claim to pizza fame, however, is that the Hawaiian pizza was invented in Canada in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a native of Greece who was running a pizzeria in Chatham, Ontario. Pineapple pizza fans unite! 🍍🥓🍕
PLAIN: In geography, a plain is a flat expanse of land that generally does not change much in elevation. The Canadian portion of the Great Plains is found in the Prairie Provinces, namely Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba.
PLAYS: Today marks the start of the Stratford Festival's 2024 season! The Stratford Festival, located in Stratford, Ontario, is North America's largest classical repertory theatre company. Each season, numerous productions take to the stage, with special emphasis on the plays of Shakespeare. The 2024 Stratford Festival lineup includes 12 plays and runs from April to October.
POKER: Canada has produced some elite poker players over the last few decades, and Toronto-born Daniel Negreanu is at the top of the list! Negreanu (aka "Kid Poker") has won 6 World Series of Poker (WSOP) bracelets and two World Poker Tour (WPT) championship titles. Other famous and successful Canadian poker players include Guy Laliberté (of Cirque du Soleil fame), Evelyn Ng, Jonathan Duhamel, Sam Greenwood, Timothy Adams, Daniel Dvoress, Mike McDonald, Sorel Mizzi, Michael Watson, and Peter Jetten.
POLKA: Polka Dot Door was a Canadian children's television series which was produced by the Ontario Education Communications Authority (later known as TVOntario) from 1971 to 1993. One of the most well-known elements of the series was the "Polkaroo", a mythical character whose name combines the words "polka dot" and "kangaroo". In 2010, the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television gave Polka Dot Door a Masterworks award, calling it a "groundbreaking children's educational series" that "changed the nature of children's television programming" and "impacted countless young Canadians and raised the international profile of the Canadian television industry."
POUND: Lobster season has officially started in Canada in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Canada currently supplies more than half of the world’s supply of “hard-shelled” Atlantic Lobster, considered one of the world’s premier seafood. A lobster pound is where live lobsters are held until they are harvested and sold, like at Halls Harbour Lobster Pound in Nova Scotia and Lobster on the Wharf in PEI, known as MacKinnon's Lobster Pound to locals.
POWER: Globally, Canada is a major energy producer. It is a top ten producer of oil, natural gas, hydroelectric power, uranium, nuclear power, biofuels and wind. Over 60% of Canada's electricity is generated by waterpower, and nuclear energy accounts for about 15% of the total Canadian electricity supply, generated at power plants in Ontario and New Brunswick.
PRANK: April Fools' Day wouldn't be the same without a classic prank, and one of the most iconic prank devices, the whoopee cushion, was invented in Toronto in the 1930s! Created by the JEM Rubber Company, this cheeky contraption has been a prankster's favourite for nearly 100 years, delivering laughs and a few embarrassed giggles along the way. A simple but brilliant invention, the whoopee cushion proves that a well-placed prank never goes out of style!
PRIVY: The Privy Council Office is the central agency of the Government of Canada which acts as the secretariat to the Cabinet of Canada and provides non-partisan advice and support to the Canadian ministry. The clerk of the Privy Council, who leads the department, is the head of the civil service of Canada, and acts as Deputy Minister to the Prime Minister.
PRIZE: The Giller Prize is the most prestigious literary prize in Canada, recognizing excellence in Canadian fiction. The prize was established in 1994 by Toronto businessman Jack Rabinovitch in honour of his late wife Doris Giller, a former literary editor at the Toronto Star.
PSALM: During the holiday season, many Canadians celebrate with music rooted in centuries-old tradition. Psalms – sacred songs and poems from the Bible – have inspired countless Christmas carols, from “O Come, All Ye Faithful” to “Joy to the World.” Singing these psalms and carols in churches, community gatherings, or around the piano keeps a centuries-old tradition alive, filling Canadian homes with festive harmony and joy.
PUPPY: The mudpuppy is Canada's largest salamander species. Found in southern Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, this unique creature spends its entire life underwater. Its feathery, dark red external gills are a striking feature and an adaptation to its aquatic lifestyle. Mudpuppies live at the bottoms of freshwater lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams, where they quietly play a vital role in their ecosystems by feeding on insects, small fish, and other invertebrates. These fascinating creatures are an important and unique part of Canada's natural biodiversity!
QUACK: Canada is a haven for duck lovers! Our country hosts over 11 duck species, and our vast network of wetlands, lakes, and marshes make it a prime stopover in the Mississippi and Atlantic Flyways, two major North American migration routes. Every spring and fall, you can witness flocks of mallards, wood ducks, and teal filling the skies and making quite the racket with their quacks.
QUAIL: Did you know that Canada is home to three fascinating types of quail: the California Quail, the Mountain Quail, and the Northern Bobwhite! These tiny birds bring big personality, whether it’s the California Quail’s fancy feather plume, the Mountain Quail’s love for sneaky hideouts, or the Northern Bobwhite’s cheerful “bob-WHITE!” call. From British Columbia’s grassy hills to Ontario’s fields, these quail are proof that even small birds can make a big impression. These small but mighty birds are a rare treat to see in the Canadian wild, so keep your binoculars handy next time you're exploring their habitats!
QUILL: Quillwork refers to the Indigenous art of using coloured porcupine quills to decorate various items such as clothing, bags, medicine bundles and regalia. Quillwork is more than just a fine example of Indigenous artisanry, it holds cultural significance as part of traditional knowledge systems. Quillwork is now a rare artform, but some Indigenous elders and artists are trying to preserve it through community-led education about quilling.
QUOTA: Fishing quotas play an important role in managing Canada’s marine resources. In 1992, the federal government placed a major moratorium on the Atlantic cod fishery after decades of overfishing led to the collapse of cod stocks, dramatically impacting communities across Newfoundland and Labrador. Since then, strict quotas and management measures have been used to help protect remaining fish populations and support the long-term sustainability of Canada’s fisheries.
RALLY: May 17 marks the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia, and Transphobia. Canada has a rich history of rallies and protests, where citizens come together to advocate for change and raise awareness about important social and political issues. The 'We Demand' rally, which took place on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario on August 28, 1971, was the first large-scale LGBTQ2+ rally in Canadian history. The rally marked a pivotal moment in Canada's LGBTQ2+ rights movement. Today, rallies and protests remain an important part of Canada's democratic process, providing a platform for citizens to voice their concerns and hold their government accountable.
RAPID: The Reversing Falls are a series of rapids on the Saint John River located in Saint John, New Brunswick, where the river runs through a narrow gorge before emptying into the Bay of Fundy. The amazing phenomenon of the Reversing Falls Rapids is a sight to behold. If you time it just right, you can watch the Bay of Fundy’s monstrously high tide reverse the flow of the mighty Saint John River.
READS: Canada Reads is an annual "battle of the books" competition organized and broadcast by Canada's public broadcaster, the CBC. During Canada Reads, five Canadian personalities champion five different books, with each advocate extolling the merits of one of the titles. The Canada Reads 2023 winner was "Ducks: Two Years in the Oil Sands" by author Kate Beaton, championed by Jeopardy super-champion Mattea Roach.
REIGN: The reign of Canada's new monarch, King Charles III, began when Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8. Queen Elizabeth II was Canada's monarch for over 70 years, making her the longest reigning monarch in Commonwealth history.
REIKI: Did you know that Reiki, a Japanese technique for stress reduction and relaxation, has found a strong following in Canada as a complementary therapy? Practised across the country in wellness centres, spas, and holistic health clinics, Reiki is embraced by many Canadians seeking relaxation and balance. Some Canadian hospitals and hospices even incorporate Reiki to support patient care. As interest in energy healing grows, Reiki has become a recognized part of Canada's wellness landscape, offering a gentle and non-invasive way to promote well-being.
REVEL: Each March 17, communities across Canada revel in the spirit of St. Patrick’s Day! From lively parades to seas of green, people across the country join in celebrating Irish heritage. In fact, Canada is home to one of the largest Irish diasporas outside Ireland, with millions of Canadians tracing at least some of their roots to the Emerald Isle.
RHINO: Did you know Canada once had a political party called the Rhinoceros Party of Canada? Founded in 1963, it became famous for its satirical and humorous platform. The party proposed outrageous policies like repealing the law of gravity and banning lousy Canadian winters. While they never gained significant political power, the party remains a quirky part of Canadian political history, known for mocking traditional politics and using humour to encourage people to think about the system in a new way.
RIDGE: The Battle of Vimy Ridge, during the First World War, is Canada's most celebrated military victory – an often mythologized symbol of the birth of Canadian national pride and awareness.
RIFLE: The Queen's Own Rifles of Canada is a Primary Army Reserve infantry regiment based in Toronto. Founded on April 26th, 1860, it is the oldest continuously serving infantry regiment in Canada. Its members have served in every Canadian military campaign and served with great distinction in World War I and World War II in which 7 Riflemen were awarded the Victoria Cross.
RIVALRY: Heated Rivalry made waves on Crave as a Canadian-produced hockey drama that blends fierce on-ice competition with an off-ice romance. Set in the world of pro hockey, the series drew major attention for its performances and LGBTQ+ representation, quickly becoming one of Crave’s most talked-about original releases. Now stars Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie have been selected as torchbearers for the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milano Cortina, carrying the Olympic flame as the Games approach!
ROBIN: The return of the robin is a sure sign of Spring in Canada! American Robins begin to arrive at their breeding grounds in southern areas of Canada in March each year. Few birds are as familiar to the Canadian public as the robin. Its plumage is easily recognizable, and it is one of the first birds to sing in the morning and one of the last to be heard at night.
ROCKIES: The Canadian Rockies are one of the most iconic mountain ranges in the world, stretching through British Columbia and Alberta. Formed over millions of years as tectonic plates collided and pushed ancient rock upward, they are part of the larger North American Rocky Mountains. Known for their dramatic peaks, glaciers, and turquoise lakes, the Rockies are home to national parks like Banff and Jasper, and attract visitors from around the globe year-round.
ROCKY: The Rocky Mountains, also known as the Rockies, are the largest mountain system in North America!
RODEO: The Calgary Stampede, Canada's largest rodeo, is billed as “The Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth”. It is held every July and turns 110 years old in 2022.
ROGER: In Canadian slang, 'hang a roger' means turn right, and 'hang a larry' means turn left. This quirky driving lingo is just one of the many fun ways Canadians put their own spin on everyday language, and it makes giving directions a little more playful!
ROPER: A roper is a person who uses a lasso to catch an animal, especially in a rodeo. The Calgary Stampede features the best riders, racers and ropers each year!
ROUND: On National Donut Day, Canadians celebrate the sweet, round treat found in bakeries and coffee shops across the country. From classic glazed rings to filled and frosted varieties, donuts are a popular indulgence enjoyed with coffee or hot chocolate. Canada is also among the highest donut-consuming countries in the world, with Canadians enjoying roughly a billion donuts each year. Their familiar round shape is part of what makes them so iconic and instantly recognizable.
ROUSE: "The Rouse" is a bugle call most often associated with the military in Commonwealth countries. It is commonly played following "Last Post" at military services. "The Rouse" was traditionally played following "Reveille", which was a bugle call played in the morning to wake soldiers up.
ROUTE: Today is the 2023 Terry Fox Run! The event is a classic Canadian tradition every Fall with communities and runners across the country coming together to fundraise for cancer research. It is the world's largest one-day fundraiser for cancer research. Terry Fox's route across Canada for his Marathon of Hope started in St. John's, Newfoundland & Labrador and ended early in Thunder Bay, Ontario, but if you stretch the total distance he ran (5,373 km) into a straight line, his route reaches all the way to Vancouver Island's west coast. You can donate to the Terry Fox Foundation in honour of Terry at terryfox.org.
ROYAL: Canada is one of the oldest continuing monarchies in the world. The title “Royal” is a sign of honour and distinction, and the granting of this distinction is a prerogative of the Sovereign. In Canada, we have the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force, the Royal Canadian Regiment in the Canadian Army, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Canadian Legion, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, and the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. In Canada's legislative process, a bill can only become law once it has received royal assent.
RUGBY: Buoyed by its inclusion in the 2016 Olympic Games, Rugby is one of the fastest growing team sports in Canada, particularly in youth and women.
SABLE: Sable Island, a remote sandbar about 300 km southeast of Halifax, is famous for its wild horses, which have roamed free for centuries! These resilient animals have adapted to the island's harsh conditions, grazing on its unusual vegetation. Sable Island is also known as the "Graveyard of the Atlantic," with over 350 recorded shipwrecks scattered along its shifting shores. Today, it is a protected National Park Reserve, with visitor access carefully managed by Parks Canada to help safeguard its delicate ecosystem. Even trees don't thrive here - except for a single Scots pine, planted in the 1960s, standing as the island's only tree!
SAILS: In Kelowna, British Columbia, the Spirit of Sail - affectionately known as The Sails - is an iconic sculpture that has become a symbol of the community. Designed by artist Robert Dow Reid and unveiled in 1978, this towering artwork stands 12 metres tall and weighs an impressive 1,820 kilograms. Located along Kelowna's waterfront, it beautifully captures the spirit of the Okanagan's connection to its lake and outdoor lifestyle. Next time you're in Kelowna, stop by for a photo - it's a must-see Canadian landmark!
SCUBA: In 1839, the Saint John, New Brunswick duo of of James Elliott and Alexander McAvity patented the "Self-contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus," which we now know as the Scuba tank. The Scuba tank revolutionized underwater exploration, allowing divers to explore the depths of the ocean without the constraints of surface connections. The invention has paved the way for ocean research, deep-sea exploration, and recreational diving. Let's give a big round of applause to the Canadian inventors of the Scuba tank!
SEDGE: In Canada, marshy areas known as sedges are important habitats for wildlife, especially for cranes! The term "sedge" not only refers to grassy wetlands but also to a group of cranes gathering in these lush areas. Canada is home to two species of cranes - the Sandhill Crane and the endangered Whooping Crane. Each fall, Sandhill Cranes flock to Canadian wetlands, where sedges provide the perfect mix of cover and food as they prepare for migration. These crane gatherings are a beautiful sight, showcasing how Canada’s diverse ecosystems support unique wildlife year-round.
SEEDS: Canada is the world's largest producer of mustard seed, most of it farmed in the southern prairie regions of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Canada is also the largest producer of flaxseed in the world, representing about 40% of world production.
SENATOR: Canada’s upper chamber, the Senate of Canada, is made up of 105 appointed senators who review laws and represent regional and minority interests. Today, most senators are chosen through a non-partisan, merit-based process, where an independent advisory board reviews applications from Canadians and recommends candidates to the Prime Minister.
SERGE: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or “Mounties,” are known for their iconic uniforms that feature the iconic scarlet tunic called a red serge.
SHALE: The Burgess Shale is a fossil-bearing deposit exposed in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia, Canada. Found in Canada's Yoho National Park, it is one of the most important fossil sites in the world! The rocks here preserve not only the usual hard shells of ancient organisms, but also soft skin and tissue, allowing for stunning impressions of the strange creatures of 500 million years ago!
SHELL: Happy Easter from Canuckle! The Vegreville egg is a giant sculpture of a pysanka, a Ukrainian-style Easter egg, in the town of Vegreville, Alberta. Designed by Canadian artist Paul Maxym Sebaliu, the egg's shell is made up of an intricate set of two-dimensional anodized aluminum tiles in the shape of congruent equilateral triangles and star-shaped hexagons. The egg is 9 metres (31 feet) long and three and a half storeys high, weighing in at 2.5 tonnes (5,512 lb) making it the largest pysanka in the world! It was constructed in 1975 in honour of the early Ukrainian settlements east of Edmonton.
SHIRT: Feb 22 is Anti-Bullying Day, also known as Pink Shirt Day, where people wear a pink-coloured shirt to stand against bullying. The initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two Nova Scotia teenagers when a fellow Grade 9 student in Berwick was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
SHOOT: In the biathlon, athletes must ski fast and shoot with precision, and Canada has excelled in this challenging sport! Myriam Bédard made history by winning two gold medals at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics in the 7.5 km and 15 km biathlon events. She also won a bronze medal at the 1992 Albertville Olympics. Bédard's remarkable marksmanship and skiing prowess have made her a Canadian legend in the biathlon world.
SIOUX: The Sioux are a group of Indigenous peoples whose traditional territories extend into the Prairies of Canada, especially in present-day Manitoba and Saskatchewan. In Canada, they are represented primarily by Dakota and Nakota Nations, with rich cultural traditions, vibrant languages, and histories of resilience. Today, Sioux communities continue to thrive, preserving their heritage through storytelling, ceremony, and a deep connection to the land.
SITKA: Sitka spruce is the largest spruce in the world, with some trees in the Carmanah River Valley on Vancouver Island in British Columbia reaching a height of 100 metres! Its range hugs the western coast of Canada and the US, continuing south into northernmost California. The San Juan Spruce is a Sitka spruce tree located in the San Juan Valley of Vancouver Island. Until a lightning strike in July 2016, it was the second largest known Sitka spruce tree by volume in the world. Canada's largest spruce is now the San Joseph Spruce, aka ‘San Jo’s Smiley'!
SKATE: Skate Canada is the oldest and largest figure skating organization in the world.
SKILL: Skills Canada is a Canadian non-profit organization dedicated to the promotion of careers in technology and skilled trades. One of their major initiatives is the annual Skills Canada National Competition. This is an Olympic-style event in which competitors from across the country take part in various skilled trades and technology contests.
SLEIGH: Sleighs have been a part of Canadian winters for centuries, helping people travel across snow-covered landscapes long before cars and snowmobiles. From sturdy horse-drawn sleighs to festive holiday sleighs, they capture the imagination and charm of the season. Today, sleigh rides remain a popular winter tradition in Canada, bringing families together to enjoy the crisp air, sparkling snow, and a little holiday magic.
SLUSH: In Newfoundland and Labrador, it’s not Christmas without slush! This shockingly easy and potent batch cocktail is a holiday must-have in the easterly province and, abandoning all cocktail etiquette, is prepared in a salt beef bucket. Christmas slush is traditionally prepared with amber rum, frozen cans of lemonade and orange juice concentrate, pineapple juice and a whole lot of sugar. Newfoundland Christmas slush encapsulates beloved tradition, a sense of community and holiday hospitality in Newfoundland and Labrador.
SONGS: The 2024 Juno Awards are taking place in Halifax, Nova Scotia tonight to honour achievements in Canadian music in 2023. The ceremony will be hosted by Nelly Furtado. The Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) votes and awards outstanding Canadian artists for their top songs, videos, and albums released throughout the year.
SPINE: Red sea urchins are the largest urchin in the world. They are spherical, covered with a tough shell bristling with pointy spines. Red sea urchins are found in the Pacific Ocean and prefer rocky, protected areas in shallow water close to shore, though occasionally they are found as deep as 100 metres. In Canada, the main fishery is located off the coast of British Columbia.
SPINY: Canada's most unique terrestrial animal is probably not what you might think. A recent study published in the journal The Canadian Field-Naturalist has found the country's most evolutionarily distinct Canadian animal is the spiny softshell turtle! These turtles can be found in Ontario and Quebec, and are one of the largest freshwater turtle species in North America. But unfortunately, they have been listed as one of Canada's rarest species for over 20 years. If we let them disappear from Canada, we would lose almost 180 million years of unique evolutionary history. This shows how important it is to prioritize the conservation of this species and its unique legacy amongst Canadian wildlife.
SPLIT: Split pea soup is an authentic French Canadian dish that is made with yellow peas, ham, and veggies. This traditional pea soup is the ultimate in Quebec-style comfort food. This early settler soup became a staple item on the menu for Quebec's settlers as it was a filling and nutritious meal that helped them survive harsh Canadian winters.
SQUID: The Canadian fishing village of Glover's Harbour, Newfoundland (formerly known as Thimble Tickle) claims to be the "Home of the Giant Squid." It earned this distinction in 1878, when a living giant squid was discovered stranded offshore. Now enshrined in the form of a "life-sized" sculpture, the world's largest squid is the subject of an annual festival, and in 2011, the sculpture was featured on a Canadian postage stamp.
STING: Today marks the start of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) regular season in Canada! The Sarnia Sting are a junior ice hockey team based in Sarnia, Ontario. They are one of the 20 teams that make up the OHL. The franchise was granted in 1969 as one of the inaugural teams of the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League. At the time, the team was located in Cornwall, Ontario and known as the Cornwall Royals.
STOUT: Happy Canadian Beer Day! During the early period of Canada’s brewing history, heavier ales, porters and stouts were the more popular brews, owing to the traditional preferences of the English, Irish, Welsh and Scottish immigrants who comprised an increasing proportion of Canada’s population following the takeover of New France by Britain in 1763.
STYLE: Style in Canada is as diverse as the country itself – from cozy winter layers to cutting-edge couture. Canada’s fashion scene celebrates creativity and identity, with Montréal’s vibrant design houses and Toronto’s Fashion Week runways leading the way. Brands like Canada Goose, Smythe, and Indigenous-owned labels such as Lesley Hampton and Section 35 show how Canadian style blends function, culture, and artistry – proof that true northern style never goes out of fashion!
SUGAR: Spring is only a few weeks away, and that means it's almost sugar season! Sugar shacks ("cabanes à sucres" in French) are cabins where sap is collected from sugar maple trees and boiled into maple syrup. In 2022, over 72 million litres of maple syrup came out of sugar shacks in Quebec, accounting for over 90% of Canada's domestic production.
SUPER: It's a Bird... It's a Plane... It's Superman! The Superman character was co-created by Canadian artist Joseph Shuster. Born in Toronto, he is a cousin of Wayne Shuster, one-half of the beloved Canadian comedy duo Wayne and Shuster. Joseph, who passed away in 1992 at the age of 78, said Metropolis was modelled on Toronto and the Daily Planet was inspired by the Toronto Star, which he delivered as a kid.
SWING: Oscar Peterson is one of Canada's most honoured musicians and is widely regarded as one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Born and raised in Montreal, Peterson began playing piano at the age of five. Known as the "master of swing" or the "king of inside swing," Peterson made a name for himself with his incredible dexterity, speed and ornate technique on the keys. Over the course of Peterson’s acclaimed career, he won seven Grammy Awards, was awarded the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario, won the Martin Luther King Jr. Achievement Award, received numerous honorary degrees, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame. A public statue of Oscar Peterson was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth II in Ottawa in 2007. Check out this Heritage Minutes video that recounts the early years of Peterson’s music career.
SYNOD: A synod is a council or assembly in some Christian denominations to discuss and decide on matters of doctrine, administration, and other church affairs. In Canada, faith and religion play a significant role in the country's cultural mosaic. The Anglican and Lutheran churches in Canada often hold synods to guide their spiritual and organizational direction, reflecting their long-standing traditions within the country's diverse religious landscape. Canada’s religious diversity is reflected in the various synods and assemblies held by different Christian communities, contributing to the rich tapestry of beliefs and practices across the nation.
SYRUP: Canada produces 71% of the world's maple syrup, 91% of it coming from Quebec.
TAFFY: Maple taffy (tire d'érable or tire sur la neige in French-speaking Canada) is a sugar candy made by boiling maple sap past the point where it would form maple syrup, but not so long that it becomes maple butter or maple sugar. It is part of traditional culture in Québec, Eastern Ontario, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. In these regions, maple syrup is boiled, poured into rows on a snow-lined tray, and rolled onto sticks to make this chewy, irresistible candy.
TAXES: Lottery & gambling winnings in Canada are treated as windfalls and are not subject to Canadian income tax. Turns out taxes aren't always certain after all!
TAXIS: Taxis have played an important role in Canadian urban history since the early 20th century, with cities like Winnipeg and Toronto among the first to introduce motorized taxi services. During World War II, Canadian taxi fleets were repurposed for civil defense – transporting supplies, volunteers, and even serving as emergency vehicles when needed. Today, while rideshares are popular, classic yellow cabs remain a familiar sight in many of Canada’s biggest cities.
TENTH: Newfoundland and Labrador became Canada’s tenth province on March 31, 1949, following a historic vote to join Confederation. Originally known simply as Newfoundland, the province was officially renamed Newfoundland and Labrador in 2001 to better reflect its mainland territory. From colourful coastal towns to rugged northern landscapes, it’s a uniquely vibrant part of Canada’s story – tenth to join, but first in East Coast charm!
THEME: "The Hockey Theme" is a Canadian piece of instrumental theme music composed in 1968 by Dolores Claman and orchestrated by Jerry Toth. The theme was associated with CBC Television's Hockey Night in Canada and it was widely recognized as Canada's unofficial second national anthem.
THING: The Nature of Things is television’s longest-running science series that debuted on CBC on November 6, 1960. It evolved into an hour-long documentary during renowned Canadian scientist and environmental activist David Suzuki’s tenure as host (1979–2023). The groundbreaking program was among the first to present scientific findings on subjects such as HIV/AIDS and climate change. Over the course of more than 60 seasons and over 900 episodes, The Nature of Things has been seen in more than 80 countries. It has received 17 Gemini Awards and seven Canadian Screen Awards.
THULE: Todayis International Inuit Day! The Thule were the ancestors of today’s Inuit, emerging around 1000 CE and migrating eastward from Alaska across the Arctic. They settled in what is now northern Canada and Greenland, adapting brilliantly to one of the world’s harshest environments. Expert hunters and innovators, the Thule developed tools such as dog sleds, harpoons, and umiaks (large skin boats). Their ingenuity and resilience laid the foundation for Inuit cultures that continue to thrive across Canada’s North today.
TIMBER: Timber is at the heart of one of Canada’s oldest and most important industries. Canada’s vast forests produce world-class timber used in construction, furniture, and paper products worldwide. From the towering pines of British Columbia to the hardwood forests of Ontario and Quebec, different regions supply wood suited for everything from framing lumber to fine cabinetry, with sustainable management helping support communities and ecosystems for generations.
TITAN: The Ottawa Titans are one of three Canadian baseball teams that play in the MLB Partner Frontier League. Formed in 1993, it is the oldest currently running independent league in the United States. The Can-Am League merged with the Frontier League in 2019.
TODAY: Today's Special is a Canadian children's television program that aired from 1981-1987. Much of the series was set in a department store based on Simpson's then-flagship location in Toronto. The magic words "Hocus pocus alimagocus!" would bring Jeff the mannequin to life on each show. The adventures of Jeff, Jodie, Sam Crenshaw and Muffy Mouse brought magic to the screen for over 120 episodes!
TOPAZ: Hidden beneath Canada's rugged landscapes, topaz can be found glimmering across the country, including in Bancroft, Ontario - Canada's 'Mineral Capital' - as well as in Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, and in British Columbia's abundant felsic plutonic rocks. This brilliant gemstone forms in granite pegmatites and can dazzle in shades of yellow and rich golden brown! Though Canada isn't a major source of gem-quality topaz, rockhounds cherish the stunning specimens unearthed in these geological hotspots.
TOTEM: The word totem comes from the Algonquian word “odoodem“ meaning “his kinship group“.
TOURS: World Tourism Day, created by the United Nations World Tourism Organization, is celebrated each year on September 27th to spread awareness about the importance of tourism and its impact on our society. Canada is a country filled with famous landmarks, historical wonders, delicious food, incredible culture, and all the outdoor exploration you could want. Whether you are touring the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, touring one of Canada's many national parks and historic sites, touring Niagara Falls, or taking a tour through the Canadian Rockies, there are so many natural and cultural wonders to enjoy in our country!
TOXIC: During the First World War, a Canadian innovation helped protect soldiers from toxic gases on the battlefield. The Hypo Helmet, invented by Newfoundland doctor Captain Cluny Macpherson in 1915, was an early type of gas mask designed to filter out toxic gases like chlorine gas. It was made of a chemically treated flannel hood with a mica visor, and was a crucial development in protecting soldiers from the harmful effects of chemical warfare. This Canadian invention was an important step in the evolution of gas masks, helping to save countless lives during the war.
TREES: One of the most widely-known facts about Canada is that we’ve got an abundance of trees, but did you know that Canada actually boasts 30 per cent of the world’s boreal forest and 10 per cent of the world’s total forest cover?
TRIBE: In Canada, Indigenous tribes, also called nations or bands, have rich cultures, languages, and histories that stretch back thousands of years. The name tribe has also inspired modern artists, such as the Canadian group A Tribe Called Red (now The Halluci Nation), who blend traditional Indigenous music with electronic beats to celebrate culture and community.
TRIKE: Aqua trikes are making waves across Canada! These big-wheeled, pedal-powered water tricycles let riders glide across lakes and ponds with ease - a fun, stable ride that’s popular with families and adventurers alike. You can find them in Collingwood, Ontario, Cardigan, Prince Edward Island, and Kelowna, British Columbia, just to name a few. Aqua Trikes give Canadians of all ages a playful, unique way to enjoy the water and the outdoors.
TRUCK: The first known dump truck was developed in Saint John, New Brunswick when Canadian Robert Mawhinney attached a dump box to a flatbed truck in 1920. His idea was an instant hit, and within a decade, the dump truck was mandatory equipment wherever earth was moved.
TURBO: The TurboTrain was an early high-speed passenger train that operated in Canada from 1968 to 1982. The TurboTrain was powered by a gas turbine engine and could attain a maximum speed of over 270 km/h. The TurboTrain was one of the first "tilting trains" to enter service in North America. It operated on the Montreal–Toronto route, and under optimal conditions was supposed to complete the trip in less than four hours, though it often took about four and a half hours.
TWICE: April 11th is National Poutine Day, and what better way to enjoy this iconic Canadian dish than with twice-fried potatoes! Most traditional poutine recipes call for the potatoes to be fried twice, creating that perfect balance of crispy on the outside and soft on the inside. This ensures the fries can hold up to the rich gravy and squeaky cheese curds without getting soggy. Whether you stick with the classic or get creative, twice-fried fries are the key to the ultimate poutine experience!
TWILL: Coast Salish peoples include a variety of First Nations living along the Northwest Pacific Coast in British Columbia. In traditional Coast Salish society, blankets held much importance. They were generally white twill-weave or twined featuring repeated geometric designs, and were thick and heavy. In addition to serving many practical functions, twill blankets were a primary medium of exchange and they held much spiritual significance.
ULTRA: Ray Zahab is a Canadian explorer, ultra distance runner, and founder of non-profit impossible2Possible. A recent recipient of the Meritorious Service Cross of Canada, Ray is an Explorer in Residence of the Royal Canadian Geographical Society, and Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. In 2015 Canadian Geographic recognized Ray as one of Canada's Top Explorers. He has ran 17,000+ km across the world's deserts, and unsupported expeditions in some of the coldest places on the planet. From ultra marathons to crossing the Sahara and beyond, Ray's journey has taught him that we can truly exceed any limits we think we might have.
UNCLE: Mon oncle Antoine (My Uncle Antoine) is a 1971 French-language Canadian drama film directed by Claude Jutra for the National Film Board of Canada. The film depicts life in a rural mining town in Québec before the Asbestos Strike of 1949. Mon oncle Antoine has twice been voted the greatest Canadian film in the Sight & Sound poll, conducted once each decade. The Toronto International Film Festival placed it first in the Top 10 Canadian Films of All Time three times.
UNION: January 11th is Sir John A. Macdonald Day! Macdonald was the first Prime Minister of Canada and one of the architects of Confederation. He was the dominant creative mind which produced the British North America Act and the union of provinces which became Canada. Both before and after Confederation in 1867, Canada used the United Kingdom's Royal Union Flag, commonly known as the Union Jack.
UNITE: Today is Commonwealth Day, a celebration of the global community of nations that are united by shared values, including democracy, peace, and respect for human rights. Canada, as a member of the Commonwealth, plays a key role in this collective effort, working alongside 55 other nations to foster cooperation and development. The Commonwealth is a diverse group, yet its members are united in their commitment to making the world a better place. From humanitarian aid to cultural exchange, Canada continues to work with its Commonwealth partners to build a more just and sustainable future.
UPPER: In Canadian history, Upper Canada (also called Canada West) was the region in Canada now known as Ontario. You can travel back in time to one of Canada's largest living-history sites and experience life in the 1860s at Upper Canada Village near Morrisburg, Ontario.
VERSE: Canada has a rich tradition of poetry, with voices from coast to coast to coast crafting verse that captures the country’s landscapes, cultures, and stories. Each April, National Poetry Month, organized by the League of Canadian Poets, celebrates this creative spirit, bringing Canadian verse to life in communities across the country. The 2026 theme, “Land & Sea,” reflects the deep connection between poetry and place that continues to inspire verse from Canadian writers everywhere.
VINES: Canada’s wine country stretches from the maritime vineyards of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia’s Annapolis Valley to Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula and west to British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley, including the sun-soaked slopes around Kelowna. Across these diverse regions, carefully tended vines thrive in climates influenced by ocean tides, lake effects, and mountain valleys. From crisp ice wines to bright whites and rich reds, Canadian vineyards prove that great wine grows at home – and that every vine carries the flavour of Canada’s unique terroir.
VINYL: Randy Bachman's Vinyl Tap radio show on CBC is two hours of music and stories from one of Canada's musical legends. Randy Bachman has been an integral part of Canada’s music scene for more than 40 years as part of The Guess Who, Bachman Turner Overdrive and as a solo artist. Vinyl Tap was previously CBC’s top rated show for 16 years and features Randy's favourite tunes and candid stories from his life on the road and in the studio.
VOCAL: Today is International Inuit Day! It is a holiday that was created to celebrate Inuit and amplify their voices. Inuit throat singing, or katajjaq, is a distinct vocal style uniquely found among the Inuit. It is a form of musical performance, traditionally consisting of two women who sing duets in a close face-to-face formation with no instrumental accompaniment. Their technique relies on short, sharp, rhythmic inhalations and exhalations of breath. The Inuit recognize katajjaniq as part of their cultural heritage.
VOTER: Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district in municipal, provincial/territorial, and federal elections. Did you know that on the day of a federal election, Elections Canada becomes the largest employer in the country? The agency hires about 250,000 people in communities across Canada.
WALLS: The only fortified city north of Mexico, one cannot visit Québec City without admiring the fortified walls and ramparts which were the city's defensive system built between 1608 and 1871.
WEDGE: The Gooderham Building, also known as the Flatiron Building, is an historic office building at 49 Wellington Street East in Toronto, Ontario. Built in 1891 to the designs of architect David Roberts Jr., it is an iconic historical structure in the heart of the provincial capital. Its wedge-like shape and distinctive colours are probably why it is one of the most photographed structures in the city!
WHEEL: La Grande Roue de Montréal is a Ferris wheel built at the Old Port of Montreal, Quebec, Canada for the festivities for the 375th anniversary of the city. Open to the public since September 1, 2017, visitors can enjoy an amazing panorama 60 metres high, four seasons a year, on the largest observation wheel in Canada.
WHIPS: Canada Whips is a Canadian resource for whip crackers worldwide. Canada Whips was formed with one specific goal in mind: to increase skill, knowledge, and participation in whip cracking across Canada and beyond! They offer tutorials, guides, glossaries, and more to whip crackers around the globe.
WHIRL: Canada's Bay of Fundy is home to the largest tidal whirlpools, thanks to its intense and unique tides. The most famous whirlpool is the Old Sow Whirlpool, located in the Passamaquoddy Bay towards the mouth of the Bay of Fundy. Old Sow is the largest whirlpool in the western hemisphere, and the second largest in the world!
WHITE: Red and white, the colours that adorn the National Flag of Canada, have undeniably come to represent Canada both at home and abroad. Red and white have truly become Canada’s national colours, through common use and collective pride, even if they are not officially enshrined in law. The "Great White North" is one of Canada's nicknames, and also used as the title of a Second City Television (SCTV) comedy sketch featuring our favourite two hosers, Bob & Doug McKenzie!
WINDS: "Four Strong Winds" is a song written by Ian Tyson and recorded by Canadian folk duo Ian and Sylvia. It was a top 10 single in Canada in 1963. The song has a clear Canadian context and subtext, including an explicit mention of the province Alberta as well as references to long, cold winters. In 2005, CBC Radio One listeners chose this song as the greatest Canadian song of all time, and is considered the unofficial anthem of Alberta.
WINDY: St. John’s tops the list of Canada’s windiest cities. With an average annual wind speed of 24.3 km/h, it feels like the wind is constantly blowing. Southern Alberta is one of the windiest regions in Canada. Second only to St. John’s, Lethbridge gets more days with strong winds than any city in Canada, while Calgary – famous for its Chinook blows – is the windiest large city in Canada.
WOODY: It wouldn't be Christmas in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia without Woody The Talking Christmas Tree! Every year between Nov 18 and Dec 23, Woody wakes up from his deep slumber for Santa's grand arrival. On the daily, shoppers young and old at the Mic Mac Mall line up and wait for Woody to wake up at noon so they can have a quick chat with him. When people are done visiting Woody, they are given a free tree sapling that they can take home and plant in their backyard to help Woody renew the forests and clean the air. Proceeds from Woody's Store, where shoppers can buy various Woody merchandise like toques, magnets, car fresheners and even a "Woody hoodie," benefit the IWK Foundation in Halifax to help families in need.
WORLD: The Toronto Blue Jays are back in the spotlight, competing in the 2025 World Series – their first appearance in over three decades! As Canada’s only Major League Baseball team, the Jays carry a nation’s hopes for another championship, just as they did with their historic back-to-back World Series wins in 1992 and 1993. From coast to coast to coast, fans are rallying behind the Blue Jays as they chase another world title for Canada!
WRIST: Ringette, invented in 1963 by Canadian Sam Jacks, is a fast-paced ice sport where players use straight sticks to control a rubber ring. The wrist shot is the most common way to score, making quick wrist movements and precise passes the heart of this uniquely Canadian game. From backyard rinks to national arenas, every goal begins with a flick of the wrist! Canuckle is excited to be sponsoring the U12A Nepean Ravens Beswick ringette team this season!
XENON: Every night of the year, the three waterfalls that make up Niagara Falls are illuminated in glowing colours creating a stunning vista that can be viewed from near and far. For over 20 years, 21 xenon spotlights illuminated Niagara Falls in a rainbow of colours. In December 2016, a brand new $4-million LED lighting grid was unveiled that delivers twice the brightness and a wider spectrum of colour, all at a quarter of the energy consumption than the previous illumination.
YEAST: December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Pale lagers are the most popular beer in Canada. Most lagers are distinguished by the use of a "bottom-fermenting" yeast that ferments at relatively cold temperatures. The term "lager" comes from the German word for "storage", as the beer was stored before drinking, traditionally in the same cool caves in which it was fermented. Celebrate the day with a lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
ZONES: There are six time zones in Canada covering four and a half hours. From west to east these time zones are: Pacific, Mountain, Central, Eastern, Atlantic and Newfoundland. Canada's Sir Sandford Fleming developed the modern system of standard time and time zones, still in use today.
